habitatDescription: The Mardon Skipper is dependent upon native fescue-dominated grasslands in Washington, Oregon, and California (Black and Vaughan, 2005).
physicalDescription: A dull yellowish and brown skipper. Rather like a washed out runty version of the common more eastern P. mystic.
globalRangeComments: Mardon skippers are known from 4 disjunct regions in the United States: 1) the south Puget Sound region in western Washington, 2) the southern Washington Cascades, 3) the southern Oregon Cascades, and 4) northwest coastal California and southwest Oregon (Kerwin 2011, Hatfield et al. 2018). They have limited dispersal capability (believed to be less than 0.8 km), and movement between these regions is unlikely (Kerwin 2011). In Washington they are known from Klickitat, Thurston, Skamania, and Yakima Counties (Kerwin 2011, Jakubowski 2015). In Oregon they are known from Curry, Jackson, and Klamath Counties (NatureServe Network 2022). In California they are known from Del Norte County (Black et al. 2013). They are suspected from Siskiyou County, California, based on the proximity of records in Jackson County, Oregon (Black et al. 2002, Miller and Hammond 2007). Miller and Hammond (2007) suggest this species historically occurred in western Oregon's Willamette Valley, but supporting records do not exist. Mardon skippers are documented on the Mount Adams and Cowlitz Valley Ranger Districts of the Gifford Pinchot National Forest, the Naches Ranger District of the Okanagan-Wenatchee National Forest, the Gold Beach and High Cascades Ranger Districts on the Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest, and on the Gasquet Ranger District of the Six Rivers National Forest. They are documented from the Coos Bay and Medford Districts of the Bureau of Land Management.
references: Pelham, J. P. 2008. A catalogue of the butterflies of the United States and Canada with a complete bibliography of the descriptive and systematic literature. The Journal of Research on the Lepidoptera. Volume 40. 658 pp. Revised 14 February, 2012.

physicalDescription: Known from males only. Wings and appendages luteus. Forewings with narrow reflexed coastal cell lined with long, slender, brown scalses. Maxillary palpi one-segmented, short, apex bearing dense brush of flattened black scales. First antennal segment long, unmodified. Spurs large, 2-4-4. Genitalia (Fig6). Tenth tergite, lateral aspect, with ventral corner produced caudad as elongate, narrow, distally truncate lobe, and acute apex directed dorsad; distal margin of dorsal portion straight, several short spines present along dorsal margin. Tenth tergum, dorsal aspect (Fig 6A), with short ,mesal incision, resultant dorsal lobes short, spinous; apices of ventral lobe project caudad beyond remainder, apex truncate. Clasper,lateral aspect, with apex subacute, curved dorsad, basodorsal lobe short and digistate, lateral lobe slender and acute. Clasper from ventral aspect (Fig 6B), with an inconspicuous, mesal lobe, short, flattened, lightly sclerotized, does not reach apex. Aedeagus short, arcuate, no ornamentation (Denning 1971).
globalRangeComments: Known from the Coast Range of Oregon and California and possibly east to the Willamette National Forest, the latter occurrence depends on identification verification

GENITALIA: Process (probably the tenth tergite) from lateral aspect sinuate, its apex slender and acute, from dorsal aspect the apex gradually curved laterad; lateral margin about midway bearing a prominent, acute, lateral structure with distal margin darkened and heavily sclerotized. physicalDescription: Microscope required. "Male: Color dark brown, slightly lighter on legs and venter. General structure typical for genus, and for subgenus as described above. Genitalia see Ross (1951). Ninth segment nearly annular, with anterior margin evenly bowed. Tenth tergite with lobes bladelike and thin, each with lateral aspect fairly shallow, triangular, elongate, and ending in a sclerotized portion which is curved ventrad and beaklike. Cercus moderately long and slender, with an irregular row of long setae. Clasper with base massive, apex tapering to a point curved sharply mesad; at the dorsal apex of the basal portion is a short sharp projection pointed mesad. Aedeagus with simple rods. Female: Size, color, and general structure as for male. Female characters typical for ophionis complex, for which means of specific separation in this sex are not yet known. (Ross 1951)."
globalRangeComments: Only known from the type locality; Rogue River National Forest, Jackson County, Oregon  (Ross, 1951).  Now likely extirpated.

globalRangeComments:
This Range Extent analysis only includes occurrences of the putative A. nuttalliana species concept by Chong et al. (2008) and excludes those of A. californiensis, a closely related species in the same clade (Mock et al. 2010, Chong et al. 2008). Reported occurrences are not always in agreement: Blevins et al. (2017) included British Columbia, Canada; Arizona, California, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Washington, Wyoming, USA; Chihuahua, Sonora, Mexico that provided a Range Extent of 2,086,110 square km. Mock (2010) and Nedeau et al. (2005) included California, Oregon, Washington, southern British Columbia; east to Utah (Burch 1975); Idaho records (Henderson, 1924; 1936) records believed to be Anodonta kennerlyi. Wyoming records were identified as A. californiensis and proposals to find extant and additional populations in the Bear River drainage using eDNA and visual surveys are expected to occur for the next couple years (L. Tronstad pers. comm. 2018). Preliminary analysis (K. Mock, Utah State University, pers. comm.) indicates Utah Anodonta are distinct from A. oregonensis of the Pacific northwest and should tentatively be assigned to A. californiensis pending future taxonomic work. Clarke (1981) cites distribution as the Fraser and Columbia River systems in southern British Columbia (absent from Vancouver Island) and south to central California.
There are reports of A. nuttalliana from Mexico; however, all of the records from Mexico available on MUSSELp Database (Graf and Kummings 2018), are presently identified as other Anodonta species (mostly A. impura) on database websites of the respective institutions where they are deposited (Field Museum of Natural History, Museum of Comparative Zoology, US National Museum, Delaware Museum of Natural History,The Academy of Natural Sciences Pennsylvania). Additionally, no other occurrences available from these institutional database websites listed Mexico as a locality for specimens identified as A. nuttalliana. This will likely remain uncertain until taxonomy has better resolution and sufficient field surveys accurately document western Anodonta species.

habitatDescription: Generally found in rather moist, rocky forested terrain, at medium-high elevations. Most often, the dominant vegetation is Pseudotsuga menziesii forest, with a rich understory including many forbs, deciduous shrubs, and bryophytes. Moist valley, ravine, gorge, or talus sites are preferred, ie on a low slope and near permanent or persistant water, but not normally subject to regular or catastrophic flooding. (Frest and Johannes, 1995; U95FRE01ORUS).
globalRangeComments: Original range included the Blue Mountains, WA and OR; a string of western ID and ID Panhandle counties (Bonner, Kootenai, Shoshone, Clearwater, Nez Perce, Idaho, and Adams); extreme NE WA (Pend Oreille and Stevens co.); and part of NW MT (Lincoln, Sanders, Lake, Mineral, Ravalli, and Missoula Cos.; river valleys involved included the upper Weiser, Little Salmon, Salmon, Hells Canyon, Coeur d'Alene, St. Joe, Clearwater, Lochsa, Selway (all Snake tributaries), Flathead, Kootenai, Clark Fork, and Bitterroot (Burke 2013, Frest and Johannes 1995). Currently known to survive at several sites in NE WA; Frest and Johannes (1995) have unsuccessfully rechecked most of the old ID sites, finding it extirpated in all but one, yet they have collected the species in several sites recently; current range therefore is unknown. Historically 13 sites in 6 counties in Montana (Hendricks, 2003) but none recently until Ward Creek in Mineral County (Hendricks, 2003). Hendricks and Maxell (2005) surveyed 108 sites in Montana and Idaho and found this species at 10 in northern Idaho (bringing total to 33) and 6 in northwest Montana (bringing total to 19).

habitatDescription: Hemphillia glandulosa inhabits relatively moist and undisturbed coniferous forest, generally at low to middle elevations. It is generally found under forest floor litter or debris and on or under logs. General habitat is moist forest dominated by conifers, but with a moderate hardwood component. The forest floor is moist, but not wet or saturated. (Frest and Johannes, 1993a).
physicalDescription: The genus Hemphillia is unique among Canadian slugs in having a distinct dorsal (visceral) hump that is covered by the mantle; the shell, a flattened plate, is visible through a slit in the mantle. The tip of the tail has a caudal mucus pore, which in some species is overhung by a fleshy protuberance, often called the caudal "horn." Hemphillia glandulosa is one of the smaller species within the genus, with adults typically ca. 20 mm. The body is depressed under the visceral hump, and behind this, the tail is raised into a prominent dorsal keel. The key feature for distinguishing slugs of this species is the presence of numerous, dense papillae that cover the mantle. The body is whitish or grey with darker markings; the tentacles and head are dark bluish; the flanks are lighter coloured. Anatomically, the inner wall of the penial stimulator is wrinkled (COSEWIC, 2003).
globalRangeComments: Ranges from Vancouver Island, British Columbia through Washington to Multnomah and Clatsop Counties, northwestern Oregon.  In Washington, known from King, Pierce, Thurston, Lewis, Skamania, Clallam, Grays Harbor, Pacific and possibly Whatcom Cos. Absent east of the Cascade Ranges in Washington and Oregon.  In Canada, known from the southern end of Vancouver Island only (14 localities as of February 2002) (COSEWIC, 2003).

physicalDescription: Body ground color light reddish gray, somewhat lighter on sides; with small, black, "spider-web" spots; spots wometimes aligning along mucus grooves of flanks, but not joining in reticulation.  Mantle of same ground color as rest of body.  Head and cephalic tentacles somewhat darker than rest of body.  Sole white, unmarked.  Foot fringe prominent, crossed by alternating light and dark stripes.  Internal shell a low-arched plate with off-center terminal nucleus; periostracal margins extending beyond calcified part of shell.  Caudal mucus pit present.  Penial retractor muscle strap-shaped, inserted at summit of penis.  Penis cylindrical, with blunt summit; containing a verge.  Verge broadly conical, nearly fillinc cavity of penis.  Atrium with thin-walled, capacious sac containing single long, curved, calcareous dart with sharp tip and slightly expanded base (Roth, 2004).

globalRangeComments: Pristiloma crateris is known from wet forested habitats at mid to high elevation sites in Clackamas, Deschutes, Douglas, Hood River, Jefferson, Klamath, Lane, Linn, Morrow, and Wasco Counties, Oregon, USA. Most records are from along the eastern and western crest of the Cascade Range, but there are a few recent (post-2000) records from the Blue Mountains and Klamath Mountains ecoregions (Roth 2015, NatureServe Network 2022). The species is documented on the Fremont-Winema, Deschutes, Willamette, Umpqua, Umatilla, and Mount Hood National Forests and the Roseburg and Northwest Oregon BLM Districts. It is suspected from the Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest (Blackburn 2017).

physicalDescription: Cryptomastix devia is the largest member of its genus with a shell diameter of 18-25 mm in adults. The species can be identified by the shell. The adult shell is pale yellowish to brown, globose-heliciform and has 56 whorls. The apertural lip is whitish, broadly expanded and recurved. There is a low bulge present on the basal lip. A prominent white, tooth-like structure (parietal denticle) is present within the aperture. There is a small umbilicus. The body of the animal is light brown and may have a lilac undertone (Kelley et al. 1999; COSEWIC, 2002). Only on reaching maturity does the apertural lip of the shell become thickened and recurved, and the parietal denticle is formed. Juveniles lack the parietal tooth and developed apertural lip. Juvenile shells have short, fine hair-like periostracal projections, but these are visible only with a minimum of 10× magnification and are often absent in dead specimens (COSEWIC, 2002).
globalRangeComments: Cryptomastix devia is currently found in the West Cascades and Puget Trough of Washington and the Cascades Mountains, Willamette Valley, and Coast Range Mountains of Oregon (Burke 2013). It was formerly found on southern Vancouver Island (COSEWIC 2002). The current range encompasses 50,000 to 80,000 km2.

Likewise, this range extent does not include specimens from Mt Hood National Forest in Oregon, which Burke believes are different taxon (Foltz-Jordan and Black 2015). habitatDescription: Found in portions of a single nasmode.  One colony occurs in rather dry sage scrub; but the areas with this species have perennial seeps, and association with very moist areas is typical.  The substrate is basalt.  (Frest and Johannes, 1995; U95FRE01ORUS).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Found in native prairie wetlands; open, grassy, with small scrub and trees, including areas subject to periodic flooding (Frest and Johannes, 1999).
globalRangeComments: Currently known from two areas in Willow Creek Park in Lane County, Oregon. It could have occurred more widely in native prairie wetlands in the Willamette Valley, Oregon.
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

county: Bent, Clac, Clat, Colu, Coos, Doug, Lane, Linn, Mari, Mult, Till, Wash, Yamh
globalRangeComments: For Washington, records indicate this species has a low-elevation distribution from Olympia to the Columbia River that does not include any National Forest. For Oregon, it is known from the Coos Bay, Eugene, Roseburg, and Salem Districts and is suspected to occur in the Medford District of the Bureau of Land Management. It is known from the Siuslaw, Umpqua and Willamette National Forests and is suspected to occur in the Mount Hood, Rogue River, and Siskiyou National Forests, and the Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area.  Specimens collected by Branson (1977; 1980) on the Olympic Peninsula have been determined to be immature haplotrematid snails (Applegarth, 2000).
references: Turgeon, D. D., J. F. Quinn, Jr., A. E. Bogan, E. V. Coan, F. G. Hochberg, W. G. Lyons, P. M. Mikkelsen, R. J. Neves, C. F. E. Roper, G. Rosenberg, B. Roth, A. Scheltema, F. G. Thompson, M. Vecchione, and J. D. Williams. 1998. Common and scientific names of aquatic invertebrates from the United States and Canada: Mollusks. 2nd Edition. American Fisheries Society Special Publication 26, Bethesda, Maryland. 526 pp.

globalRangeComments: This species occurs in the Blue and Wallowa Mountains of northeast Oregon and far southeast Washington, USA. It is documented on the Umatilla and Wallowa-Whitman National Forests in Oregon. It is suspected present on the Umatilla National Forest in Washington, and on Bureau of Land Management Spokane District in Washington, and Vale and Prineville Districts in Oregon. Frest and Johannes (1995) were unable to locate the species at a number of sites in the Blue Mountains between 1991-1994, including at the type locality.
references: Turgeon, D. D., J. F. Quinn, Jr., A. E. Bogan, E. V. Coan, F. G. Hochberg, W. G. Lyons, P. M. Mikkelsen, R. J. Neves, C. F. E. Roper, G. Rosenberg, B. Roth, A. Scheltema, F. G. Thompson, M. Vecchione, and J. D. Williams. 1998. Common and scientific names of aquatic invertebrates from the United States and Canada: Mollusks. 2nd Edition. American Fisheries Society Special Publication 26, Bethesda, Maryland. 526 pp.

globalRangeComments: This species occurs in the United States in northwestern Montana, northern Idaho, in northeastern Washington and the Blue Mountains of southeastern Washington as well as northeastern Oregon (Hendricks 2003; RARECAT 2025; InvertEBase 2025).
references: Turgeon, D. D., J. F. Quinn, Jr., A. E. Bogan, E. V. Coan, F. G. Hochberg, W. G. Lyons, P. M. Mikkelsen, R. J. Neves, C. F. E. Roper, G. Rosenberg, B. Roth, A. Scheltema, F. G. habitatDescription: This type locality is in a moderately steep basalt creek canyon with short basalt cliffs and small-scale talus piles in some areas. Fairly open Pinus ponderosa and Pseudotsugua menziesii forest with some deciduous understory and common grasses characterize the type locality. (Frest and Johannes, 1995; U95FRE01ORUS).
references: Frest, T.J. and E.J. Johannes. 1995c. Interior Columbia Basin mollusk species of special concern. Final Report (contract #43-0E00-4-9112) prepared for Interior Columbia Basin Ecosystem Management Project. Deixis Consultants, Seattle, Washington. 274 pp. + tabs., figs.

habitatDescription: Found in moderately xeric, rather open and dry situations, in large scale basalt (or sometimes metasedementary) taluses on steep, cool (generally N-facing) aspects, generally associated with springs and seeps, although not found in wettest areas. (Frest and Johannes, 1995; U95FRE01ORUS).
globalRangeComments: Endemic to Oregon (Gaines pers. comm., 1996).
references: Turgeon, D. D., J. F. Quinn, Jr., A. E. Bogan, E. V. Coan, F. G. Hochberg, W. G. Lyons, P. M. Mikkelsen, R. J. Neves, C. F. E. Roper, G. Rosenberg, B. Roth, A. Scheltema, F. G. Thompson, M. Vecchione, and J. D. Williams. 1998. Common and scientific names of aquatic invertebrates from the United States and Canada: Mollusks. 2nd Edition. American Fisheries Society Special Publication 26, Bethesda, Maryland. 526 pp.

habitatDescription: Occurs mostly in basalt talus piles and at the base of basalt cliffs, generally north and east-facing.  Typically small permanent springs and seeps are associated, although this species avoids the wettest areas.  Surrounding areas gererally have sage scrub.  (Frest and Johannes, 1995; U95FRE01ORUS)
references: Frest, T.J. and E.J. Johannes. 1995c. Interior Columbia Basin mollusk species of special concern. Final Report (contract #43-0E00-4-9112) prepared for Interior Columbia Basin Ecosystem Management Project. Deixis Consultants, Seattle, Washington. 274 pp. + tabs., figs.

habitatDescription: A strong xerophile, found on several lithologies in sage scrub; but particularly common on limestone.  Most colonies occur in small-scale, north-facing talus or rock piles.  This species generally occurs at lower elevations in major stream valleys. (Frest and Johannes, 1995; U95FRE01ORUS).
references: Frest, T.J. and E.J. Johannes. 2000a. An annotated checklist of Idaho land and freshwater mollusks. Journal of the Idaho Academy of Science, 36(2): 1-51.

habitatDescription: Found in basalt landslides, sometimes with brush cover; partial riparian association.  The type locality area originally included a spring, but road building and quarrying has destroyed this.  (Frest and Johannes, 1999)
globalRangeComments: This species is known from near Sutherlin, Oregon, south to Redding, California, USA. Records are known from Jackson, Josephine, Douglas Counties in Oregon and Shasta County in California. There is also one disjunct 2016 record from eastern Humboldt Co, California. Specimens from Douglas Co, Oregon, may be a new, undescribed species (Barry Roth pers. comm., 2019). This would restrict the estimated range of H. hertleini to 20,000 sq km, but would not change the range extent rating.
references: Turgeon, D. D., J. F. Quinn, Jr., A. E. Bogan, E. V. Coan, F. G. Hochberg, W. G. Lyons, P. M. Mikkelsen, R. J. Neves, C. F. E. Roper, G. Rosenberg, B. Roth, A. Scheltema, F. G. Thompson, M. Vecchione, and J. D. Williams. 1998. Common and scientific names of aquatic invertebrates from the United States and Canada: Mollusks. 2nd Edition. American Fisheries Society Special Publication 26, Bethesda, Maryland. 526 pp.

habitatDescription: Lower elevations. Basalt talus, often north facing, often associated with seeps and springs (N95FRE01ORUS).
physicalDescription: Gray (1834) description in latin. Shell umbilicated, orbicularly subconoid, epidermis light yellow or brownish on upper surface, with a black or chestnut-colored revolving band visible on the four outer whorls, the lower surface dark chestnut, sometimes uniformly black; suture distinct, impressed; whorls 7, rounded, spirally striate, with minute, delicate, impressed lines, the striae of increase very distinct, and occasionally with rows of tubercles running obliquely to the striae of growth, bearing very distinct raised lines under the epidermis, quite like prostrate hairs; peristome reflected below, simple above, thickened; aperture ovate, banded within; umbilicus open, a little contracted by the reflection of the peristome; base flattened-convex (Binney 1985).
globalRangeComments: This subspecies occurs in the lower Deschutes River valley and Columbia River Gorge in Oregon and near The Dalles in Washington, USA (Frest and Johannes 1993; Oswald et al. 2021; Washington Natural Heritage Program 2004; Oregon Biodiversity Information Center 2019).
references: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. 1989a. Endangered and threatened wildlife and plants; animal notice of review. Federal Register 54(4):554-579.

habitatDescription: Found mostly in dry, north-facing basalt taluses along permanent streams and in the vicinity of springs and seeps , at low elevations.  Taluses are comparatively loose and open but partial cover by bryophytes.  (Frest and Johannes, 1995; U95FRE01ORUS).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Generally in deciduous trees and brush in wet, relatively undisturbed forest, at low elevations; also coastal scrub (Frest and Johannes, 1999).
globalRangeComments: This subspecies occurs in Curry and Douglas Counties in southwestern Oregon, USA (Burke 2013; Fallon et al. 2015; GBIF 2024).
references: Richardson, L. 1982. Helminthoglyptidae: Catalogue of species. Miscellaneous publications of the Department of Malacology of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia. Number 6.

habitatDescription: Relatively low elevations in comparatively undamaged, somewhat dry and open forested terrain (Frest and Johannes, 1999).
globalRangeComments: This subspecies occurs in southwestern Oregon (Oregon Biodiversity Information Center 2016).
references: Richardson, L. 1982. Helminthoglyptidae: Catalogue of species. Miscellaneous publications of the Department of Malacology of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia. Number 6.

habitatDescription: Reported at 1600 ft elevation near the Salmon River, 12 miles from Mount Hood. The anatomy and ecology are essentially unknown. (Frest 1989).
globalRangeComments: This subspecies is found in and around the Columbia River Gorge in Oregon and Washington (Burke 2013; Oregon Biodiversity Information Center 2016).
references: Richardson, L. 1982. Helminthoglyptidae: Catalogue of species. Miscellaneous publications of the Department of Malacology of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia. Number 6.

habitatDescription: This species occurs generally in moderate elevation, very cold springs and spring-fed small streams. Sites are very cold, clear, have moderate to swift flow, and sand, gravel, an cobble substrate. (Frest and Johannes, 1995).
globalRangeComments: Baker and Grant Counties, Oregon.
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

globalRangeComments: This tentative species is known from both sides of Upper Klamath Lake, including the Link River, in Klamath Co., Oregon (Frest and Johannes, 1995).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Occurs on undersides of cobbles and boulders and of very large Nostoc colonies in spring-influenced sites in a large lake and a large, spring-influenced creek (Frest and Johannes, 1998)
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Occurs on undersides and sides of cobbles and boulders in spring complex draining into Upper Klamath Lake and rarely in spring-influenced outflow from lake (Frest and Johannes, 1998).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: This species is known only from the type locality at unnamed springs, Cricket Creek, Silvies River drainage.  The type locality is composed of a series of small, cold rheocrenes.  (Hershler, 1999).
globalRangeComments: This species is known from two widely distributed locations in Lake and Harney Counties Oregon. The type locality is a series of unnamed springs near Cricket Creek in Harney County (Hershler 1999). A record from Malheur County (near Warm Springs Canyon) was determined to be in error (VanNorman pers. com.) and is not included in the range extent.
references: Hershler, R. 1999. A systematic review of the Hydrobiid snails (Gastropoda: Rissooidea) of the Great Basin, Western United States. Part II. Genera Colligyrus, Eremopyrgus, Fluminicola, Pristinicola, and Tryonia. The Veliger, 42(4): 306-337.

habitatDescription: Found in medium springs. Sites with this species have slow-swift flow, clear, very cold water. Substrate varies from sand and mud to basalt cobble and boulder, with most specimens occurring in areas with coarse substrate. (Frest and Johannes, 1999).
physicalDescription: A small snail of springs with a broadly conical shell.
globalRangeComments: Endemic to the USA and known from specimens in southern Oregon (Klamath Co. and Lake Co.) and northern California (Lassen Co., Modoc Co. and Shasta Co.) (Hershler and Frest 1996, Hershler 1999)
references: Turgeon, D. D., J. F. Quinn, Jr., A. E. Bogan, E. V. Coan, F. G. Hochberg, W. G. Lyons, P. M. Mikkelsen, R. J. Neves, C. F. E. Roper, G. Rosenberg, B. Roth, A. Scheltema, F. G. Thompson, M. Vecchione, and J. D. Williams. 1998. Common and scientific names of aquatic invertebrates from the United States and Canada: Mollusks. 2nd Edition. American Fisheries Society Special Publication 26, Bethesda, Maryland. 526 pp.

globalRangeComments: Once thought to inhabit the entire Columbia valley, but as revised by Hershler and Frest (1996), only found in lowermost Willamette River, and possibly lower Columbia River below Portland, Oregon. This species could be extinct; as 1991 and 1994 surveys in the vicinity of Willamette Falls failed to find any specimens (Hershler and Frest, 1996); and former habitat is now highly industrialized.
references: Turgeon, D. D., J. F. Quinn, Jr., A. E. Bogan, E. V. Coan, F. G. Hochberg, W. G. Lyons, P. M. Mikkelsen, R. J. Neves, C. F. E. Roper, G. Rosenberg, B. Roth, A. Scheltema, F. G. habitatDescription: This cold spring snail tends to avoid very small springs. The species prefers gravel-cobble substrate and feeds on perilithon (Frest, 1992).
globalRangeComments: Widely distributed in the northwest Great Basin in California, Nevada, and Oregon (Hershler 1999).
references: Turgeon, D. D., J. F. Quinn, Jr., A. E. Bogan, E. V. Coan, F. G. Hochberg, W. G. Lyons, P. M. Mikkelsen, R. J. Neves, C. F. E. Roper, G. Rosenberg, B. Roth, A. Scheltema, F. G. Thompson, M. Vecchione, and J. D. Williams. 1998. Common and scientific names of aquatic invertebrates from the United States and Canada: Mollusks. 2nd Edition. American Fisheries Society Special Publication 26, Bethesda, Maryland. 526 pp.

habitatDescription: Found in large cold spring complexes, with mixed mud-gravel substrate (Frest and Johannes, 1999).
globalRangeComments: According to Frest and Johannes (1996) it is only known from one site in the Lost River drainage in Oregon.
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Exceptionally large cold springs and their outflows; excellent water quality, gravel-boulder substrate, very cold and clear flowing water (Frest and Johannes, 1999).
globalRangeComments: Appears to be restricted to two large spring complexes in the Klamath River system in southwestern Oregon (Frest and Johannes 1999).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Occurs in large cold exceptionally pristine springs and their outflows, including medium-sized creeks (Frest and Johannes, 1999).
globalRangeComments: Likely confined to the middle Klamath River drainage in Jackson County, Oregon and Siskiyou County, California (Frest and Johannes 1999).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: This species occurs in Klamath Lake, a few major trubutaries, and part of the Klamath River, generally in areas with gravel-boulder substrate, spring influx, and some flow.  Prefers clear, cold, oligotrophic flowing water.  (Frest and Johannes, 1999).
globalRangeComments: Known from the middle and upper Klamath River in California and upper Klamath Lake and spring-fed tributaries in Oregon (Frest and Johannes 1996). It could have been formerly widespread but is now absent from impounded areas.
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Found in small-large spring complexes, generally with mixed mud-gravel substrate.  Most sites are comparatively open, in dry Ponderosa pine forest.  (Frest and Johannes, 1996).
globalRangeComments: Currently known from a few springs near the Lake of the Woods and in the Lost River drainage in Oregon (Frest and Johannes 1996).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Found only in springs or strongly spring-influenced portions of a medium-sized river. The species seems to prefer cold, clear water, coarse (gravel-cobble) substrate, and slow to swift constant flow. (Frest and Johannes, 1998).
globalRangeComments: Currently restricted to several springs in the Lost River drainage in Oregon (Frest and Johannes 1996).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Found in small-large spring complexes, generally with mixed mud-gravel substrate (Frest and Johannes, 1998).
globalRangeComments: Harney and Malheur Counties, Oregon.
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: This species is found in large springs and spring-fed creeks, generally very cold, clear, and oligotrophic.  The substrate ranges from silt to cobbles; basalt is the predominant source.  (Frest and Johannes, 1995; U95FRE01ORUS)
globalRangeComments: Jefferson County, Oregon.
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

globalRangeComments: Appears to be restricted two creeks in the Klamath River system in southwestern Oregon. Surveys of springs in surrounding drainages have not found this taxon (Frest and Johannes 1999).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Found in small-large spring complexes and runs, generally with mixed mud-gravel substrate.  Most sites are in rather open meadow or in sparse Ponderosa pine forest.  (Frest and Johannes, 1996).
globalRangeComments: Currently restricted to three springs in the Odessa Creek area in Oregon (Frest and Johannes 1996).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Found in a single small-large spring complex, with mixed mud-gravel substrate (Frest and Johannes, 1996).
globalRangeComments: Currently known from two sites on Upper Klamath Lake in Oregon (Frest and Johannes 1996).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Confined to large undisturbed, very cold oligotrophic springs draining into upper Klamath Lake (Frest and Johannes, 1999).
physicalDescription: A small (5 mm) snail with tall conical spire-shaped shell and evenly black body, tentacles, and mantle.
globalRangeComments: Endemic to the USA and known only from Oregon (Klamath Co.) in large spring-influenced habitats in the upper Klamath River drainage. Range extent based on the 9 existing records is 2477 square km.(Liu and Hershler 2019, GBIF 2023).
references: Liu, H-P., and R. Hershler. 2019. A new species and range extensions for three other species of pebblesnails (Lithoglyphidae, Fluminicola) from the upper Klamath basin, California–Oregon. ZooKeys 812 (2019):47-67.

habitatDescription: Occurs only in medium-large oligotrophic cold, clear springs generally with common wood fragments; mud-cobble substrate.  Sites are generally in rich, partly open meadows and edges of Ponderosa pine forest, with abundent sedges and grasses.  Springs are generally associated with bogs or marshes.  Water depth is shallow, and moderate to swift flow is characteristic.  (Frest and Johannes, 1996).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Very large cold springs and their outflows; exceptional water quality, gravel-boulder substrate (Frest and Johannes, 1999).
globalRangeComments: Known from two springs in adjacent creeks in the Klamath River drainage in southwestern Oregon (Frest and Johannes 1999).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Occurs in large cold springs and strongly spring-fed streams.  Typically, these are oligotrophic, clear, rather swift, and have stable sand-cobble substrate.  Area bedrock is basalt.(Frest and Johannes, 1995; U95FRE01ORUS)
globalRangeComments: Wasco County, Oregon.
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Found in small-large spring complexes, generally with mixed mud-gravel substrate.  Most sites are well shaded, in a largely closed, rich Ponderosa pine forest.  (Frest and Johannes, 1996).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Found in medium-large cold spring complexes and spring-influenced stream, generally with mixed mud-gravel substrate.  Most sites are well-shaded, in largely closed, rich Ponderosa pine forest.  (Frest and Johannes, 1996).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Small, undisturbed cold springs and outflow (Frest, 1995).
globalRangeComments: Endemic to type locality in Page Springs in the Donner and Blitzen River drainage in Oregon (Hershler 1999).
references: Hershler, R. 1999. A systematic review of the Hydrobiid snails (Gastropoda: Rissooidea) of the Great Basin, Western United States. Part II. Genera Colligyrus, Eremopyrgus, Fluminicola, Pristinicola, and Tryonia. The Veliger, 42(4): 306-337.

habitatDescription: Large-lake hydrobiid, now surviving only in areas with spring influence to counter eutropification and subsequent periodic low DO2.  This taxon prefers areas with gravel-boulder substrate and few macrophytes (Frest and Johannes, 1998).
globalRangeComments: Klamath basin, Oregon and Pit River drainage, California (Hershler et al., 2003). Populations of Pyrgulopsis intermedia from the Pit River basin formerly assigned to this species were recently transferred to Pyrgulopsis archimedis (Hershler et al., 2003).
references: Turgeon, D. D., J. F. Quinn, Jr., A. E. Bogan, E. V. Coan, F. G. Hochberg, W. G. Lyons, P. M. Mikkelsen, R. J. Neves, C. F. E. Roper, G. Rosenberg, B. Roth, A. Scheltema, F. G. Thompson, M. Vecchione, and J. D. Williams. 1998. Common and scientific names of aquatic invertebrates from the United States and Canada: Mollusks. 2nd Edition. American Fisheries Society Special Publication 26, Bethesda, Maryland. 526 pp.

habitatDescription: Spring-influenced areas along the Lost River system (Frest, 1998, pers. comm.).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Found on cobbles and boulders in spring-influenced areas of a large lake.  (Frest and Johannes, 1995; U95FRE01ORUS).
references: NatureServe. Unpublished. Concept reference for taxa which have not yet been described; to be used as a placeholder until a citation is available which describes the circumscription of the taxon.

habitatDescription: Pyrgulopsis fresti is distributed along a short reach of the Owyhee River above Three Forks.  It lives on loose cobble and basalt rock faces in very shallow, thermal spring runs (Hershler and Liu, 2009).
globalRangeComments: This recently described species is distributed along a short reach of the Owyhee River above Three Forks. Additional surveys of seeps and springs along the Owyhee River in southeastern Oregon will be needed to accurately delineate the geographic range of this species (Hershler and Liu, 2009).
references: Hershler, R. and H.-P. Liu. 2009. New species and records of Pyrgulopsis (Gastropoda: Hydrobiidae) from the Snake River basin, southeastern Oregon: Further delineation of a highly imperiled fauna. Zootaxa 2006:1-22.

habitatDescription: Occurs primarily in large springs, but also in spring-influenced creeks and rivers, generally with gravel-boulder substrate (Frest and Johannes, 1993). Medium- large cold springs. Springs with this species have common Rorippa, sand, gravel, and cobble (basalt) substrate, are cold and clear, and have moderate velocity. (notes for now-synonymized Pyrgulopsis sp. 11, Malheur springsnail, Frest and Johannes, 1995; U95FRE01ORUS).
globalRangeComments: Burch (1989) cites distribution as Owyhee River, Malheur Co., Oregon. Hershler (1994) listed southern Oregon in Crooked Creek, Owyhee River drainage (Snake basin); Barren Valley (internal drainage), lower Klamath Lake basin; and in northeast California in the Pit River below Fall River (Taylor, 1985). Populations from the Pit River basin formerly assigned to this species were recently transferred to Pyrgulopsis archimedis (Hershler et al., 2003). Hershler and Liu (2009) modified Oregon distribution to Crooked Creek (Owyhee River basin), Barren Valley (Great Basin), plus new records from the Crooked Creek headspring and along the lower Owyhee River, southeastern Oregon extending the range about 65 km north of its type locality into the lower Owyhee River basin.
references: Turgeon, D. D., J. F. Quinn, Jr., A. E. Bogan, E. V. Coan, F. G. Hochberg, W. G. Lyons, P. M. Mikkelsen, R. J. Neves, C. F. E. Roper, G. Rosenberg, B. Roth, A. Scheltema, F. G. Thompson, M. Vecchione, and J. D. Williams. 1998. Common and scientific names of aquatic invertebrates from the United States and Canada: Mollusks. 2nd Edition. American Fisheries Society Special Publication 26, Bethesda, Maryland. 526 pp.

habitatDescription: Perennial seepages and rivulets, where protected from seasonal flushing in the rainy season.  According to Davis (1967), lives on shallow mud banks and marsh seepages leading into shallow streams.  (Frest and Johannes, 1999).
globalRangeComments: This species is a southwest Oregon and northwest California coastal endemic. It has a large north to south (600 km) range extent and narrow (39 km) east to west extent.
references: Turgeon, D. D., J. F. Quinn, Jr., A. E. Bogan, E. V. Coan, F. G. Hochberg, W. G. Lyons, P. M. Mikkelsen, R. J. Neves, C. F. E. Roper, G. Rosenberg, B. Roth, A. Scheltema, F. G. Thompson, M. Vecchione, and J. D. Williams. 1998. Common and scientific names of aquatic invertebrates from the United States and Canada: Mollusks. 2nd Edition. American Fisheries Society Special Publication 26, Bethesda, Maryland. 526 pp.

habitatDescription: Semiaquatic.  The snails are characteristically found among wet leaf litter and vegetation besides flowing or standing water in shaded situations where humidity remains high (Frest and Johannes, 1999).
globalRangeComments: It is restricted to coastal regions of Oregon and California (van der Schalie and Dundee, 1955; Taylor, 1981). Burch (1989) cites distribution as San Francisco and Oakland, California; and Bolinas Bay, Marin Co., California.

physicalDescription: Accentric conical shell up to 0.5 inches long, 0.4 inches wide, and 0.2 inches high (Neitzel and Frest 1989). Shell small, solid, roundly ovate, slightly broader posteriorly, high-arched, apex posterior; finely concentrically striate, depressed conic (Hannibal 1912). "Shell coarse, somewhat ponderous, wide, ovate, elevated; lines of growth conspicuous; apex eroded, placed far back: anterior and lateral slopes convex, posterior slope steep and rectilinear. Color opake chesnut-brown. Dimensions: 8mm long, 6.25mm wide, 3 mm high."

physicalDescription: The Great Basin Rams-horn has a rather stout shell, diameter approximately 13 mm; whorls do not increase rapidly in width, but body whorl larger with simple aperture offset downwards at steep angle. Periphery on shoulder is sharply angular, keeled; spire not concave, but slightly convex, open umbillicus (Baker 1945).
globalRangeComments: This species occurs in Idaho, Wyoming, Utah, Nevada, Oregon, and California, USA, where it is generally confined to lake and large spring complexes on the periphery of the Great Basin. Burch (1989) cites three subspecies, Helisoma newberryi newberryi from Idaho, Utah, Nevada, Oregon, and California; Helisoma newberryi jacksonensis from Jackson Lake, Wyoming (from Henderson, 1932), and Helisoma newberryi occidentale from Eagle Lake, Lassen Co., California (from Hanna and Henderson, 1934). There are few remaining populations; most are in the Upper Klamath Lake and Pit River drainages, northeastern California and south central Oregon (see Frest and Johannes 1995; 1998). Taylor and Smith (1982) cite Pliocene assemblages from Honey Lake, in Lassen Co., California. Koehler (1995) lists late Pleistocene assemblages from the Dolomite site, Owens Lake, Inyo Co., California. Frest and Johannes (1995b) further list occurrences for subspecies jacksonensis as several sites in and in the immediate vicinity of Jackson Lake, Co., Wyoming, including areas in Grand Teton National Park but note no live specimens have been collected in recent years and relocation efforts were unsuccessful.

habitatDescription: This snail inhabits a narrow zone of inter-tidal habitat on glasswort/pickleweed salt marshes at the edges of bays and estuaries where fresh and ocean waters mix.  It lives on the stems of Salicornia, and possibly some other marsh plants.  It also lives on substrates such as woody debris and rocks beneath vegetation. (MacDonald 1969)
physicalDescription: Shell thin, turbinate with four or five rounded whorls; apex sub-acute, last whorl somewhat inflated, subrimate, with or without three or four longitudinal brown bands; aperture ovate, outer lip thin, inner lip appressed to the columella and somewhat thickened; suture deep; epidermis greenish. Operculum with nucleus subcentral with two and one-half whorls (Hemphill 1877).
globalRangeComments: This common cold-water North Pacific marine gastropod has a southernmost limit in North America in Humboldt Bay, California; but occurs from there north to the Gulf of Alaska and from there westward throughout the Aleutian Island chain, the Pribilof and Commander (Komandor) Islands, over to the east coast of Kamchatka, and in Russia south to the Kurile Islands (Reid, 1996).  In the U.S. it is currently known only from Humboldt Bay, California; Coos Bay, Oregon; and Gray's Harbor, Washington (Jones, 1977; Taylor, 1981); but more localities undoubtedly exist and it was initially incorrectly thought to be a different species.

globalRangeComments: Cryptomitrium tenerum is an amphitropical disjunctive species, which occurs in western North America, Central America, and western South America. In the United States, it occurs in western Washington, western Oregon, and California; in Mexico, it occurs in Baja California, Chihuahua, Jalisco, Morelos, and Mexico states; it also occurs in Panama, central Chile, the province of Salta, Argentina, and Taiwan. The range extent in North and South America was estimated to be 11.6 million square kilometers using herbarium specimens and photo-based observations documented between 1982 and 2023, 140 million square kilometers if Taiwan is also included (Katagiri and Deguchi 2011, Wang et al. 2011, Gradstein 2017, Arrocha et al. 2021, CNABH 2023, GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023).

This species is known from Alaska, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut, south to the subalpine regions of California, with questionable reports from Greenland; it is also found in northern and central Europe and Siberia (Stotler and Crandall-Stotler 2017).

It has recently been found in Kamchatka, Russia, extending the range past Alaska into northeast Asia (Godfrey and Godfrey 2008), with Kamchatka included, the range extent is 1,850,000 square kilometers, with only the North American locations the range extent is 970,000 square kilometers.

globalRangeComments: Andreaea schofieldiana is endemic to the Pacific Northwest of the United States in southwestern British Columbia south to Siskiyou and Del Norte Counties in California (Christy and Wagner 1996, Christy et al. 2022). There is a report from Fresno County, California, which extend the range of this species; range extent is calculated with and without this specimen. Most specimens from Oregon were determined to be another species of Andreaea but one specimen, not yet reviewed, may be this species (J. Christy and L. Wise, pers comm., 2023).

globalRangeComments: Interruptedly circummontane; in North America, known from unglaciated mountains in Alaska, Yukon, northern British Columbia, western Alberta, and Saddle Mountain Oregon (Horton 1983). globalRangeComments: Leioderma sorediatum has a paleotropical distribution, and is most commonly found in New Zealand and Australia, but is absent from the southern Indian Ocean. In the Pacific it occurs in Hawaii and disjunctly in the Pacific Northwest of the United States, Canada and Ecuador (Galloway and Jorgensen 1987). It is most abundant in disturbed areas and forest edges, and has been found from sea level to 2600m.

"In Africa it is a frequent species mainly in the east and southern parts.  It occurs in southwestern Europe as far north as Great Britian and Ireland (nowadays rare), in France, Spain, and Portugal.  Also known from the Mediterranean Islands of Corsica, Sardinia, and Sicily.  In Asia it is found in India, Sri Lanka, Malasia, Vietnam, Indonesia, China, Taiwan, and Japan.  In the new world, in Newfoundland, USA, Caribbean Islands, Mexico, Central America and throughout South America, from Colombia to Chile.  Ecuador and Peru at high elevations.  In Australia, Queensland, New South Wales and Tasmania, New Zealand and the Pacific Islands including Hawaii" (Almborn 1989).

habitatDescription: Open, rocky ridges and talus slopes. Coarse gravel substrate (granodiorite and basalt lithosol). Restricted to the subalpine or alpine zones of montane regions. In mosaic of open area and scrubby coniferous forest of Abies lasiocarpa, Picea engelmannii, Pinus albicaulis and Pseudotsuga menziesii in the Elkhorns. In the Wallowas, open ridge in Festuca viride-Koeleria cristata community. Associated species include: Arenaria capillaris, Claytonia megarhiza var. bellidifolia, Draba paysonii var. treleasii, Geum rossii, Haplopappus greenei, Heuchera cylindrica var. alpina, Luzula parviflora, Oxyria digyna, Sedum roseum, Trisetum spicatum, Castilleja glandulifera, Selaginella watsonii, Ivesia gordonii.
physicalDescription: Dwarf plant, only 2 cm tall; yellow flowers in condensed umbels that have a ring of fused green bracts beneath the flower heads. Unique in the Apiaceae because it has simple, undivided leaves.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Occurs on open, exposed, windswept slopes and summits in both full sun and in shade of Tsuga mertensiana and Pinus albicaulis. Grows in red, calcareous rock of sedimentary soils of the Hurwall Formation. Always occurs in rocky areas with rocks ranging from small, gravel sized particles to larger, shale like pieces. Area resembles alpine tundra with dwarf plants, exposed rock and with little soil development. All aspects and slopes were noted although the majority occur on moderate slopes, 2-15%. Only a few plants were noted on steep, exposed south facing slopes.
physicalDescription: Small, woody based perennial 2 to 7 in tall (5-18 cm).  Foliage is blue- green in color.  The 1 to 2 1/2 inch long leaves (3-6 cm) are cut into 1/2 by 1/8 inch segments (.3 -1.27 cm). Two to five small yellow flowers are clustered in compact, flat-topped heads on stems with a few small leaflets.  The oval-shaped seed is about 1/8 inch long (.3 cm) with a narrow paper thin margin surrounding.

ecologyComments: Grows on basalt substrate.
globalRangeComments: Smooth Desert-parsley (Lomatium laevigatum) occurs in the western United States. It is endemic to the Columbia River Gorge in southern Washington (Klickitat County) and northern Oregon (Sherman and Wasco counties). It occurs along or near the Columbia River from the Dalles, Oregon on the west end to the John Day Dam on the east end, approximately 25 mile stretch. Range extent was estimated to be about 1233 square kilometers, using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1994 and 2025 (Fertig and Kleinknecht 2020, RARECAT 2024, GBIF 2025, iNaturalist 2025, NatureServe 2025, SEINet 2025, WNHP 2025).

habitatDescription: Mid- to low elevation canyon grasslands, ranging from very steep to relatively gentle slopes and dominated by one to four bunchgrasses. Grassland and shrubland associations, range from late to very early seral stages of succession. L. rollinsii have been recorded from the following associations by Johnson and Simon 1987: very early Agsp-Spcr-Arlo3 (dominated by Aristida longiseta), early Agsp-Spcr-Arlo3, Feid-Kocr (low), Feid-Agsp/Phco2, Agsp-Poa, Spcr, Glne/Agsp, Rhgl/Agsp.
globalRangeComments: Rollins' Lomatium occurs in the northwestern United States, in the vicinity of the Snake River Canyon and Salmon River Canyon in Asotin County, in southeastern Washington, in Baker and Wallowa counties, in northeastern Oregon and Nez Perce, Lewis, and Idaho counties, in western Idaho. The range extent is estimated to be 10,580 square kilometers (NatureServe 2022, SEINet 2022).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Lomatium serpentinum is known from the Snake River drainage in southeastern Washington, western Idaho, and eastern Oregon (WNHP 2023). Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1982 and 2023 (CPNWH 2023, GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023, NatureServe 2023).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

ecologyComments: Open areas or openings in thinly-wooded hillsides in scrub oak-ponderosa pine communities. Stony, clay poorly developed soils. Reported associates include: Quercus garryana, Balsamorhiza sagittata, Lupinus spp., Lomatium columbianum, L. nudicaule, Hydrophyllum capitatum var. thompsonii, Allium acuminatum and Rhus diversiloba.
globalRangeComments: Suksdorf's Desert-parsley (Lomatium suksdorfii) occurs in the western United States; it is endemic to the lower Columbia River in the East Cascades in Klickitat County, Washington and Wasco and Hood River counties, Oregon. Range extent was estimated to be 1300 square kilometers, using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1994 and 2025 (RARECAT 2024, GBIF 2025, iNaturalist 2025, NatureServe 2025, SEINet 2025, WNHP 2025).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Lomatium watsonii is endemic to the northwestern United States east of the Cascade Range, along the eastern foothills, from central Washington (Chelan, Kittitas, Yakima, and Klickat counties) south to north-central Oregon (Gilliam, Hood River, Jefferson, and Wasco counties) (FNA 2024, Giblin and Legler 2026, OSU 2026). Range extent was estimated to be approximately 17,000 square kilometers using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data documented between 1994 and 2025 (RARECAT 2025, GBIF 2026, iNaturalist 2026, NatureServe 2026, SEINet 2026).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Occurs along the margins of vernal pools in the Agate Desert, usually with native forbs and introduced annual grasses. In the Illionis Valley, it occurs in moist alluvial floodplains, with native bunchgrasses (Poa scrabrella and Danthonia californica) adjacent to Pinus ponderosa - Quercus garryana savanna with Ceanothus cuneatus and Arctostaphylos species. || Wet meadows at edges of dry serpentine pine forest in Josephine County, and margins and bottoms of vernal ponds in Jackson County.
physicalDescription: Lomatium cookii is a perennial herb, about 6" to 20" tall, with yellow flowers, a leafless stem, smooth leaves and large, corky thickened fruit.
ecologyComments: Occurs in vernally wet habitats. Blooms and fruits early in the spring. Able to survive experimental burns quite well. At one site, disturbance (leveling of the soil), created a narrow band of soil over the rock bottom, mimicing the vernal pool margins - and leading to the only population of the plant in a non-natural setting.
globalRangeComments: Lomatium cookii is a narrow, local endemic restricted to two counties in the southwestern portion of Oregon, USA. It is limited to two small areas: the Agate Desert area north of the city of Medford, Jackson County, and the Illinois River Valley area near Cave Junction, Josephine County. Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1993 and 2024 (iNaturalist 2024, NatureServe 2024, OBIC 2024, OSU 2024, SEINet 2024).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Dry, moderately steep, south-facing slopes of sandy-stony soil and talus, derived from granodiorite. Between shrub-steppe (dominated by Cercocarpus ledifolius and Artemisia tridentata) and subalpine woodland (dominated by Pinus albicaulis and Picea engelmannii). Associated species include: Lupinus caudatus, Polygonum phytolaccaefolium, Castilleja applegatei, Haplopappus lyallii, Linum lewisii, Lomatium cusickii, Viola purpurea, Pteryxia terebinthina, Kellogia galioides, Phlox austromontana, and Trisetum spicatum.
ecologyComments: Grows in loose clusters or as regularly spaced individuals.
globalRangeComments: Lomatium erythrocarpum is endemic to the Elkhorn Range which spans Baker, Union, and Grant Counties, Oregon, U.S.A. Range extent was estimated at 8 km2 using a convex hull polygon applied to herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1993 and 2024 (CPNWH 2024, NatureServe 2024, SEINet 2024).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Lomatium packardiae occurs in the northwestern United States, in the northern Great Basin. It occurs in Grant, Harney, Malheur, and Lake counties in southeastern Oregon, Humboldt and Washoe counties in northwestern Nevada, and Canyon, Owyhee counties, in southwestern Idaho, it is also reported from Cassia and Washington counties in Idaho, but these collections need further verification of their identity. The range extent is estimated to be 36,500 square kilometers (Cronquist 1992, NatureServe 2023, SEINet 2023).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1999. A synonymized checklist and atlas with biological attributes for the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. First edition. In: Kartesz, J.T., and C.A. Meacham. Synthesis of the North American Flora, Version 1.0. North Carolina Botanical Garden, Chapel Hill, N.C.

habitatDescription: Occurs on scree, talus gullies, and slopes with seasonal water runoff, above and at the limit of tree growth. Vegation is sparse but associated species include Picea breweriana, Pinus monticola, Tsuga mertensiana, Penstemon spp., & Carex breweri.
globalRangeComments: Mt. Shasta Arnica occurs in the northwestern United States, in the Cascade Range and Klamath Range of northern California and western Oregon. It has an intermittent range, occurring in rocky alpine and subalpine habitat north from the Mt. Shasta area (in Shasta, Siskiyou and Trinity counties) of California to the southern Oregon Cascades (occuring in Deschutes, Douglas, Klamath counties). The range extent was estimated to be 27,000 square kilometers, using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1992 and 2023 (CCH2 Portal 2023, Flora of North America Editorial Committee 2006, GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023, NatureServe 2023).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Rocky, sandy and cobbly shoreline and banks of rivers.
physicalDescription: A taprooted biennial or perennial herb growing 4 to 16 inches tall (1-4 dm). Densely silky hairy leaves grow in crowded persistent or deciduous rosettes at the base of the plant. The leaves measure 1 to 4 inches long (2-10 cm) by 1/3 to 1 1/2 inches wide (.7-4 cm) in outline but are cut two to three times into linear divisions. Stem leaves are similar but smaller and less divided. Small flowers grow in a densely clustered spikes; crowded leaf-like bracts located immediately below each flower are about 1/10 inch tall.
globalRangeComments: Restricted to the Columbia Basin Province in Washington and, formerly, Oregon. Only two natural occurrences of this variety remain in Washington, separated by 325 river km and three large hydroelectric dam/reservoir complexes (Priest Rapids Dam, McNary Dam, and John Day Dam). At least three, possibly as many as eight, extirpated Oregon sites have been documented, in Sherman (element occurrence), Multnomah (element occurrence), Hood River (WA NHP 1997), Wasco (WA NHP 1997), and Umatilla (Oregon State University Herbarium 2007) counties. These sites are periodically re-surveyed, but plants have not been found. It is likely that disturbances due to the construction of several dams and subsequent flooding of habitat resulted in the extirpation of these occurrences (Carlson 1997 and Rush 1999 cited in McCracken 2007). The Oregon Department of Agriculture (ODA) Native Plant Conservation Program initiated reintroduction efforts into the former Oregon range in spring 2008, planting material propagated from the Grant County, WA occurrence at one site in Wasco County, OR. ODA believes that the following criteria must be met before these plantings can be considered part of the extent of occurrence: a minimum of five years of stable (and sufficiently high) plant numbers, evidence of reproduction and recruitment, and sufficient confidence that site management is appropriate (K. Amsberry pers. comm. 2008). Range extent is difficult to estimate with only two known sites. Arbitrarily assuming that plants might grow up to 150 m from the river's edge on either bank yields an estimate of just less than 100 square km (110 square km if the reintroduction site is included); arbitrarily setting the range extent equal to the area of the river itself between the known sites (since plants also occur on river islands) yields an estimate of 4500 square km (4800 square km if the reintroduction site is included). Reports of this variety from Canada, California, and Greenland (Kartesz, pre-1997 datasets) are erroneous; in his published 1999 floristic synthesis, Kartesz accepts only the Oregon and Washington reports for this plant.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

ecologyComments: Riparian habitat, maintained as partially open by seasonal flooding. This species does not compete well in deep shade.

physicalDescription: Discoid Goldenweed is a low, rounded shrub with leafy stems that are 15-40 cm tall. Leaves are lance-shaped, widest above the middle, 1-3 cm long, and wavy-margined. The leaves and the inflorescence are glandular, the while stem is densely white-hairy. Flowering heads are borne in clusters of 1-3 at the ends of the branches. The glandular-hairy involucral bracts are 8-15 mm long, and the outer are broader and more leafy than the inner. Ray flowers are lacking. The 10-25 disk flowers are yellow and 8-11 mm long. The achenes have numerous, fine bristles on top.
globalRangeComments: The range of this variety is from se. OR to sw. MT, south to CA and UT. The range of this species as a whole is c. ID, sw MT, south to CA, UT, and CO. Peripheral.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Occurring along rocky streamsides and on steep walls, in moist crevices often near seepage, and at lower elevations in coniferous forest. Associated species: Mimulus cardinalis, Mitella sp., Saxifraga spp., Boykinia elata, and Poa sp. Rock size is an additional factor that determines the distribution of the target species within meta-igneous formations. The species is limited to massive rock outcrops. It is absent from the boulder to gravel sized alluvial deposits. In addition the species requires a fairly moist environment. It grows best around seeps or in small depressions in the bedrock that act as catch basins. Light to heavy shade is another important component of the species' habitat.
globalRangeComments: This daisy grows in southwestern Oregon (Josephine and Curry Counties) and adjacent northern California (Del Norte, Siskiyou, and Trinity Counties).

globalRangeComments: Erigeron disparipilus occurs in the northwestern United States in northeastern Oregon (Wallowa County), southeastern Washington (Asotin, Columbia, Garfield Counties), and western Idaho. There is some uncertainty in the identifications of specimens in southern Idaho. In addition, some populations in that region may be hybrids between Erigeron nanus and E. disparipilus indicating that hybridization occurs (FNA 2006b). Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1992 and 2023 (GBIF 2023, NatureServe 2023).

globalRangeComments: Erigeron davisii occurs in the western United States, and is a regional endemic of southeastern Washington (Asotin and Garfield counties), northeastern Oregon (Wallowa County), and west-central Idaho (Lewis, Idaho, Nez Perce counties) (MNHP 2022, FNA 2006). In Washington, It is known only from the Blue Mountains ecoregion (MNHP 2022).

habitatDescription: Inhabits moist, often rocky places, on protected slopes within mixed coniferous forests at elevation up to 1200 m. Assoc. species: Pseudotsuga menziesii, Acer glabrum, A. macrophyllum, Holodiscus discolor, Abies procera, & Rubus parviflorus
physicalDescription: Often found in clusters of plants with several stems rising from a rhizome. Perennial, 20-50 cm tall. stems mostly hairless but a little hairy under the flower heads. Leaves thin, smooth,and shiny green, lower leaves with egg-shaped blades abruptly contracted to a petiole, upper leaves strongly clasp the stem at their bases. There is one flower head per stem which has loose, glandular involucral bracts. Flower heads include a yellow central disk 12-20 mm wide, comprised of disc florets with distinctly flared corollas 4-5 mm long. The central disk is surrounded by 30-50 white ray florets, each 13-25 mm long and 2-4 mm wide. Fruit is an achene with 5 asymmetrical nerves and a pappus of 20-30 bristles (Meinke 1982, WA HP 2003, Oregon Flora Project 2007).
globalRangeComments: Erigeron howellii is endemic to the central portion of the Columbia River Gorge in Washington and Oregon. It is known from Skamania County, Washington and Clackamas, Hood River, and Multnomah Counties, Oregon (WAHP 2003, OBIC 2024). Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1993 and 2024 (GBIF 2024, iNaturalist 2024, NatureServe 2024,CPNWH 2024).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

Range extent was estimated to be over 11 million square kilometers using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data documented between 1993 and 2024 (GBIF 2024, iNaturalist 2024, NatureServe 2024, SEINet 2024).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Grows on rocky substrate on steep open or sparsely wooded slopes with little or no soil. Populations can be found above the riparian zone to the ridgetop. On lower slopes the plant is more commonly found on rock outcrops in open forested stands populated by Pinus ponderosa, Pseudotsuga menziesii, Cercocarpus ledifolius, Amelanchier alnifolia and Abies concolor at higher elevations. Above the forested slopes, plants can still be found growing around rock outcrops but also talus field, especially in draws. Other associated species include: Chrysothamnus nauseosus and Apocynum androsaemifolium, Festuca idahoensis, Agropyron spicatum, Bromus tectorum, Linum perenne, Berberis repens, Sedum stenopetalum, Clarkia pulchella, Lomatium triternatum, Eriogonum compositum var. compositum, E. heracleoides var. angustifolium, and E. umbellatum var. stellatum. This species is not restricted to serpentine substrate as has been written; more typically found on Blue Mountain shale formation.
ecologyComments: Not found in area with recent ground fires. This species may be intolerant to fire.
globalRangeComments: Luina serpentina is narrowly endemic to one area of eastern Oregon in Grant County (Peck 1961, Meyers et al. 2020).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Malacothrix sonchoides occurs in western North America from Oregon south to California, east to New Mexico, and north to Wyoming in the United States (FNA 2006). Range extent was estimated to be 1.1 million square kilometers using herbarium specimens documented between 1983 and 2024 (SEINet 2024).

physicalDescription: Desert Dandelion is a taprooted annual with milky sap and a basal rosette of leaves giving rise to one to several erect or ascending stems that are 1-3 dm high. The basal leaves are up to 10 cm long, have petioles, and are deeply pinnately divided into toothed and pointed lobes. The few stem leaves are reduced upwardly. The foliage has sparse long hair when young but is glabrous with age, other than the sparse, glandular hairs in the inflorescence. The several stalked flower heads arise from reduced upper leaves, or bracts, in an open inflorescence. Flower heads nod in the bud but become erect in flower. Each is 8-13 mm high with 2 series of involucral bracts, the outer of which is very short, and the inner of which is long-pointed. Rays are yellow and ca. 1 cm long, and disk flowers are lacking. The cylindrical achenes are 5-ribbed, 3-4 mm long, and topped by a pappus of numerous unbranched, white bristles that are united at the base and fall as one when seeds mature.
globalRangeComments: WY, east-central ID, and south-central MT to se. OR, south to AZ, NV, and possibly CA. Disjunct.

habitatDescription: Inhabits slopes or flat ground with varying exposures, in rocky serpentine soils. Occurs in grassy openings of Jeffrey pine savannas. Associated with Senecio hesperius, Festuca idahoensis, Stipa lemmonii, Calochortus howellii, Danthonia californica, and Ceanothus pumilis. Other species found in the habitat include Arctostaphylos viscida and Ceanothus cuniatus.
ecologyComments: Fire supression may be limiting the habitat for this species.
globalRangeComments: Microseris howellii is "known only from exposures of peridotite in Josephine County, Oregon" in the northwestern United States, mostly in the Illinois River Valley but also in the Lower Rogue and Applegate Subbasins (FNA 2006, OBIC 2018). Range extent was estimated to be 2,184 square kilometers using NatureServe Network occurrence data documented between 1990 and 2025 (RARECAT 2024, NatureServe 2025).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Occurs in open, bare, clay soiled sites in Oregon white oak or ponderosa pine savannas. (At Siskiyou pass it occurs in the very unusual oak-western juniper-pine habitat type). Also occurs in openings in chapparal (buckbrush or sticky manzanita) and Lemmon's needlegrass or Idaho fescue grasslands, or Douglas fir woodlands.
ecologyComments: Most natural habitats are openings created by gophers or other small mammals. It also occurs in artificial disturbances such as powerlines and roadsides with bare soil. However, many natural savannas and open chapparal areas in the region have become woodlands, with shading limiting populations of this taxa. In spite of the fact that it favors disturbance, fire supression is limiting habitat.
globalRangeComments: Taxon exists only in Oregon, near the California border.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Rafinesquia californica occurs in western North America, from Oregon south to California and east to Utah and Arizona in the United States south into Baja California and Sonora, Mexico (FNA 2006, Villasenor 2016, UNHP 2024). Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1994 and 2025 (RARECAT 2024, GBIF 2025, iNaturalist 2025, NatureServe 2025, SEINet 2025).

habitatDescription: Inhabits generally dry, clayey ash deposits subject to occasional flash flooding at ca. 1200m elevation. Associated species: Allium parvum, Phacelia lutea, Eriogonum novonudum, Trifolium owyheense, and Mimulus cusickii.
globalRangeComments: Senecio ertterae occurs only in the United States, in eastern Oregon. It is endemic to a tiny portion of eastern Malheur County, Oregon, near the Owyhee River. It is mainly within a BLM Area of Critical Environmental Concern. It's total range is about 200 sq. km (NatureServe Network Database as of March 2021, SEINet 2021).

Associated species: Festuca idahoensis, Danthonia californica, Stipa lemmonii, Microseris howellii, Calochortus howellii, Ceanothus pumilis, Horkelia sericata, and Arabis aceolata. Shrubs include Ceanotus cuneatus and Arctostaphylos viscida.
ecologyComments: Fire supression has resulted in reduction of habitat.
globalRangeComments: Illinois River Valley in southern Josephine County, Oregon.

habitatDescription: Found only on the top of a broad hill above surrounding flats. The soil is derived from volcanic tuff layered with thin crusts of limestone. The surrounding soils are derived from basalt. Assoc. species: Artemisia tridentata, Chrysothamnus nauseosus, C. viscidiflorus, Salsola kali, and most recently, Bromus tectorum.. The closest similar substrate is miles away. S. malheurensis seems to be one of the few species able to survive near harvester ant hills.
physicalDescription: Annual, up to 6 dm (2 ft) tall with a basal rosette of glabrous leaves; stem single, much branched, with scale-like leaves; flower heads numerous, clustered or single on short stalk; florets 5-11 per head; pink, white or rarely, orange-yellow, in color.
ecologyComments: The population size of this plant fluctuates greatly from year to year, affected by precipitation levels. S. malheurensis maintains its taxonomic distinction by an inbreeding mode of reproduction, genetically isolating it from its parent, an outcrosser.
globalRangeComments: Stephanomeria malheurensis occurs in the western United States where it is endemic to central Harney County, Oregon, in an area called the Narrows, near Malheur and Harney lakes.

habitatDescription: Big Sage/bluebluebunch wheatgrass-Sandberg bluegrass community. Slopes and aspect vary, rarely on north slopes. Elev. 610-1240 meters. Soils are shallow, mesic, slightly acidic derived from metasedimentary rocks.
physicalDescription: Large herbaceous perennial Happlopappus, mostly glabrous, having clasping stem leaves and large, yellow headed flowers which occurs in bunchgrass habitats.
ecologyComments: Fire supression and native bunchgrass declines have altered most habitats for H. radiatus.
globalRangeComments: Pyrrocoma radiata is endemic to the northwestern United States where it is known only from the southern end of the lower Snake River Canyon and its associated tributaries in eastern Oregon (Baker and Malheur counties) and western Idaho (Washington County), in the Blue Mountains and Snake River Plain ecoregions (FNA 2006, ODA 2010, OSU 2026). ecologyComments: In edaphic, open habitats.

habitatDescription: Occurs in areas of natural and man-made disturbance, edges and openings in woodlands and forests, both in second and old-growth, and shaded roadsides. Associated species: Pseudotsuga menziesii, Castanopsis chrysophylla and Arbutus menziesii.|| Along edges and openings in woodlands, and in open woods of mixed oak-Douglas fir-madrone, Douglas fir forests and mixed conifer forests.
physicalDescription: A perennial, mostly 2-4 feet tall, from a stout base. The lowest leaves are small and somewhat scale-like. The leaves are largest near the middle; they get gradually smaller near and in the inflorescence. The leaves, which are attached directly to the stem without petioles, are dull green and may or may not have irregular teeth. There are several leafy flower heads, which are about 1/2 inch wide. The heads do not have ray flowers (Gamon, 1986).
ecologyComments: Habitats are largely successional. Fire probably maintained these habitats before European settlement.
globalRangeComments: This species is endemic to western Oregon in the northwestern United States, west of the Cascade Mountains and mostly in the Willamette and Umpqua valleys where it has been documented in Douglas, Jackson, Josephine, Lane, and Line counties (FNA 2006, NatureServe 2025, OSU 2025). Three populations/collections in California previously identified as E. vialis have been examined at a molecular level and determined by Green et al. (2020) to be E. glabratus instead; there are no confirmed occurrences in California as of their study. Range extent was estimated to be 13,794 square kilometers using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data documented between 1994 and 2025 (RARECAT 2024, GBIF 2025, iNaturalist 2025, NatureServe 2025, SEINet 2025).
