habitatDescription: Aster curtus occurs in open grasslands (undisturbed and disturbed) at low elevations, from about 55 to 75 m (150 to 250 ft.), in the Willamette Valley ecoregion. Associated species include: Viola adunca, Potentilla sp., Prunella vulgaris, Deschampsia cespitosa, Aster chilensis spp. hallii, Festuca rubra, Erigeron decumbens, Danthonia californica.
physicalDescription: A 4-12 inch tall (1-3 dm) plant with leafy stem and a single, compact terminal cluster of flower heads with yellow central disk flowers and white to blue ray flowers.
ecologyComments: All known habitat in Oregon are successional, and are becoming closed canopy forests. They are invaded by ash, Scots broom and Douglas fir. The habitats were historically maintained by fires.
globalRangeComments: Sericocarpus rigidus is a regional endemic of the Pacific Northwest, occurring from southwest British Columbia (restricted to southern Vancouver Island) in Canada, and the Puget Trough in Washington and Willamette Valley, Oregon in the United States. This species is considered non-native in California. Range extent was estimated using NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1984 and 2025 (RARECAT 2024, NatureServe 2025).

habitatDescription: Amsinckia carinata grows on upper slopes of tufaceous hills, mostly on southern exposures, in soil covered with several decimeters of cobble, heavy gravel and or rock fragments.  Associated plants include: Eriogonum strictum, Amsinckia tessellata, Penstemon sp., Atriplex sp., and Bromus tectorum.  A. tessellata is dominant on the lower slopes of the hillsides.
physicalDescription: Annual herb about 4"-12" tall, bristly, hairy, and unbranched. Flowers are deep yellow or orange, about 3/8" long and arranged in a coil. The fruits (nutlets) are smooth, lustrous, dark gray, with some darker markings, no smaller than 3/16". The nutlet is roundish, but slightly concave on one side, with a sharp ridge on the other side.
ecologyComments: The species occurs on barren, exposed ash hill with exposed rock, talus or gravel, and constant rock-soil movement.
globalRangeComments: This plant only occurs in eastern Oregon, in the United States. It is known only from rocky hills in the Harper Valley area near the Malheur River, in northern Malheur County, Oregon.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

physicalDescription: Cryptantha is an herbaceous perennial which forms clumps of 5-30 cm high stems that arise from a branched rootcrown. The clustered basal leaves are narrowly spoon-shaped, 1-6 cm long, and covered with straight hairs that arise from swellings on the surface. Stem leaves are narrower and somewhat shorter. Flowers are borne on coiled stalks in the axils of the uppermost leaves, or bracts. These stalks expand, become slender, and spread outward as the fruits mature. The white flowers have a short, tubular corolla, which is 2-4 mm long and has 5 spreading lobes. The small crests, or fornices, at the base of the petal lobes are yellow. The 5-lobed calyx is hairy and becomes 6-13 mm long in fruit. The 4 lance-shaped nutlets are 3-5 mm long, 2-3 mm wide, and are bumpy or wrinkled, more so on the outside face. The style is less than 1.5 mm longer than the mature nutlets.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits sandy sagebrush slopes, sometimes moist slopes in ravines, at elevations between 630 to 750 m. and nearly always on north facing slopes. Associates are Artemesia tridentata, Oryzopsis hymenoides, Agropyron spicatum, Atriplex spinosa, Bromus tectorum, and many other associates.
physicalDescription: Perennial, growing 8 to 26 inches tall (2-6.5 dm), this forget-me-not relative has white flowers tinged blue. Flowering stems are hairy above and hairless below. Leaves that grow at the base are usually evergreen, hairy, 2 to 8 inches long (6-21 cm) and narrow, not much more than an inch wide (3.5 cm) with long stalks. Stem leaves get progressively smaller up the stems.
ecologyComments: This species occurs mostly in climax associations, but also exists in early and mid-successional communities. It also appears to tolerate some of the disturbance caused from cattle grazing but was not observed in areas that were heavily disrupted with signs of erosion
globalRangeComments: Hackelia cronquistii is found mainly near the eastern border of Oregon in Malheur and Baker Counties, and adjacent Idaho in Payette County. Not in Nevada per J. Kagan. Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1993 and 2024 (CPNWH 2024, NatureServe 2024, SEINet 2024).

The racemes are paired and are without bracts. The individual flowers are about 3/8-5/8 inch wide (Gamon and Kagan 1985).

habitatDescription: Inhabits areas that are seasonally wet associated with grasslands and vernal pool habitats at ca 500 to 650 m. Information available is nebulous.
globalRangeComments: Plagiobothrys figuratus ssp. corallicarpus is only known from the United States, in southwestern Oregon. It is endemic to the Sams Valley area near the city of Medford, in Jackson County and around Grants Pass, Josephine County, Oregon. The range extent is 2300 sq. km (NatureServe Network Database as of March 2021).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Boechera davidsonii occurs in western North America from Oregon and California east to Nevada in the United States (FNA 2010). Range extent was estimated to be over 160,000 square kilometers using herbarium specimens, NatureServe Network occurrence data, and photo-based observations documented between 1983 and 2024 (GBIF 2024, iNaturalist 2024, NatureServe 2024, SEINet 2024).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Boechera hastatula occurs in the western United States where it is endemic to Oregon and known only from Grant, Linn, and Wallowa Counties, in three disjunct population centers. In Wallowa County it is known from a small (<10 mile) stretch along the eastern edge of Hells Canyon, and from one isolated population in the Eagle Cap Wilderness Area of the Wallowa Mountains. Populations in Linn County are about 250 miles to the west in the western Cascades. Between these two regions, it is found in the Blue Mountains of Grant County.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Prefers rocky bluffs and cliffs between ca. 225 and 380 m. Assoc. species: Lilium washingtonianum, Belphinium trollifolium, Pityrogramma triangularis, and Sedum sp.
ecologyComments: The ability of A. koehleri var. koehleri to effectively return after disturbance appears minimal. The few known populatins are small & the plants scattered, suggesting specialized reproductive requirements.
globalRangeComments: Variety koehleri is endemic to the Umpqua River drainage near Roseburg, Douglas county, Oregon.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: This taxon is restricted to serpentine soils. Assoc. species: Arctostaphylos spp., Ceanothus prostratus, C. cuneatus, Pinus ponderosa, and Libocedrus decurrens.
ecologyComments: Restricted to serpentine soils.
globalRangeComments: Occurs in Oregon and California.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Open rocky areas, outcrops and cliffs, with little associated vegetation.
physicalDescription: A short-lived perennial plant, usually about 4-12 inches tall, with pink to purple flowers borne at or near the ends of the stalks.  Stem leaves, 2-8, simple and entire; basal leaves, spatulate, appearing smooth and shiny,  slightly toothed, forming a rosette.  Seeds pods about 1.5 inches long.
globalRangeComments: Occurs in the Siskiyou mountains of Curry and Josephine counties, Oregon. In California, the species is reported from Del Norte, Mendocino, Siskiyou, and Trinity counties.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Found on exposed slopes of ca. 150 to 450 m elevation, in dry, serpentine soils. Assoc. species: Arctostaphylos sp., Mimulus sp., Eriogonum sp.
ecologyComments: This species, as well as other uniquely adapted endemic rockcress of sw OR & n CA are a fascinating product of rapid evolution. The relationship of these taxa to each other & remaining elements of this genus is not yet understood.
globalRangeComments: Regional endemic; Rogue River canyon near Galice, Josephine County, Oregon and in Napa and Siskiyou Counties, California.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Has been observed to grow in open, grassy balds and roadsides; dry open ridges with some brush; openings in oak and pine flats
globalRangeComments: Boechera atrorubens is endemic to the northwestern United States in north-central Oregon (Wasco County) and central Washington (Kittitas and Klickitat counties), on the east slope of the Cascades Mountains (FNA 2010, Hitchcock and Cronquist 2018, Giblin and Legler 2025, OSU 2025, Washington Field Guides 2025). "Additional reports from southeastern Washington in Asotin, Chelan, Columbia, Douglas, Garfield, Grant, Okanogan, Skamania, Whatcom, and Yakima counties...are based on misidentifications of Boechera sparsiflora or other rockcress species" (Washington Field Guides 2025). Range extent was estimated to be 750 square kilometers using NatureServe Network occurrence data documented between 1994 and 2025, increasing to 4700 square kilometers when historic occurrences (greater than 30 years old) are included (GBIF 2025, iNaturalist 2025, NatureServe 2025, RARECAT 2025, SEINet 2025).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Ocuurs on dry, rocky (pumice) or sandy slopes, from mid elevations up. Typically in sparse pine or hemlock forest, with Vaccinium sp., Penstemon spp., and Erysimum sp.
physicalDescription: A perennial herb with numerous slender 10-50 cm stems that are hairy below. Basal leaves have dense branched hairs; the few stem leaves are egg-shaped to oval, with lower leaves hairy to upper leaves often smooth. Flowers are on hairless, horizontally spreading stalks and have spoon shaped petals that are rose to purplish. Fruits are spreading to more or less recurved, 2-7 cm long. Flowers from May to August.
globalRangeComments: Boechera horizontalis is endemic to Crater Lake National Park, Oregon, USA (FNA 2010). Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1993 and 2024 (iNaturalist 2024, NatureServe 2024, OSU 2024, SEINet 2024).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

Also on grassy balds, gravel of small creeks & shaded north slopes with summer ocean fogs at 840-960 m.|| Grassy balds, moist cliffs, rock crevices and gravelly streambanks.

habitatDescription: Inhabits hard, white, clayey playas ca. 950-1700 m, with few assoc. except for occasional perennial Atriplex spp., Astragalus calycosus, and Allium anceps. The sites are poorly drained and often inundated by standing water in early spring. These playas do not show alkali deposits.
physicalDescription: Low growing, slender-stemmed mustard with white, sometimes purple flowers.
ecologyComments: Grows in clay playas, characterised with deep mud cracks and being very slick when wet. Population within a playa appear to be distinct from other playa sites.
globalRangeComments: Southwestern Idaho (Ada, Owyhee, Twin Falls and Elmore Counties) and adjacent Malheur County, Oregon.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits moist areas, may be seasonal, such as river bars, lake margins, irrigation ditches, meadows, near springs,intermittent streams, at lower to mid elevations. Usually found in Artemisia sp. community types. Populations along the Columbia River occur alone or with Artemsisia lindleyana. Reported plant associates from south-central Oregon include Camissonia tanacetifolia, Dowingia sp., Arnica chamissonis, Rorippa curvisiliqua, Mimulus guttatus, and Ranunculus occidentalis. Other reported species are Salix, Ribes aurea, Iva, Elymus, Potentilla, Heliotropium cuassavicum, Sarcobatus vermicultus, Distichlis stricta, and Sessuvium verrucosmum.
ecologyComments: Appears to be limited to verally wet areas.
globalRangeComments:
Endemic to Washington, Oregon, and California, in two geographically distinct regions: (1) gravelly shores of the Columbia River in Washington and Oregon, and (2) seasonally wet areas in the high desert in south-central Oregon and northern California. On the whole, the species' range is predominantly east of the Cascade Range; along the Columbia River, however, it occurs in two segments: the arid Hanford Reach east of the Cascades, and the cooler, wetter Lower Columbia Reach west of the Cascade Crest (WA NHP 2003). Range extent is approximately 50,000 square km if the two population clusters are considered separate and approximately 150,000 square km if the are considered together.

The distribution of Rorippa columbiae appears to be related to the Columbia River lava plateau (Stuckey 1972). According to Stuckey (1972), R. columbiae was part of a very old group of plants that once was widespread and variable when western North America had more wet habitats. As the region became increasingly arid, populations were isolated and diverged morphologically. One line of morphological divergence was in the region of the Yellowstone River (R. calycina), one was in the region of Lake Tahoe (R. subumbellata) and one was on the basaltic lava formation of the Columbia River (R. columbiae). Today, these three species are isolated relics of the once abundant and widespread taxon (Stuckey 1972).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Stanleya confertiflora occurs in the northwestern United States in southwestern Idaho and eastern Oregon where it has been documented in Owyhee, Washington, Payette, and Gooding counties, Idaho and Baker, Harney, and Malheur counties, Oregon (FNA 2010, Mancuso et al. 2019). Range extent was estimated to be 28,462 square kilometers using NatureServe Network occurrence data documented between 1994 and 2025 (RARECAT 2024, NatureServe 2025).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits dry, serpentine slopes, from ca. 650 to 950 m, in open pine woods or brushy areas. Associated species: Ceanothus cuneatus, Arctostaphylos viscida, Eriogonum pendulum, and Lomatium howellii.
physicalDescription: Perennial plant, usually with unbranched glaucous (whitish and pale purple) stems. The leaves are somewhat fleshy, and are rounded at the tips with petioles. The flowers are maroon to purple, the fruits are long and narrow, 3 mm wide and 6-12 cm long (Flora of North America Editorial Committee 2010).
globalRangeComments: Streptanthus howellii is strictly endemic to serpentine in the Siskiyou Mountains of northwestern California and southwestern Oregon, in Del Norte County, CA and Curry and Josephine Counties, OR . The total range extent including historic records is 2400 km sq and the range based on herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe network occurrence data collected between 1994 and 2025 is 1100 km sq (GBIF 2025, iNaturalist 2025, NatureServe 2025, CNDDB 2025, SEINet 2025, OSU 2025). Historical reports from Siskiyou County, California, may be based on vague location information referring to the Siskiyou Mountains.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Valley bottomlands, meadows and open flats. Soils were alkaline playa clay with an occasional sandy top layer. Associated species: Chrysothamnus spp, Salsola kali, Atriplex spp, Sitanion hystrix, & Bromus.
globalRangeComments: Collections have been made from Lake and Klamath Counties in Oregon and Colusa, Lake, Lassen, Napa, Siskiyou, Trinity and Shasta Counties in California. Most of the population is centered in southern Klamath County and Siskiyou County.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Occurs in seasonal stream channels and wet areas, usually with western Juniper. Often in canyons, near or under junipers, but occasionally in dry washes, seasonal waterfalls, and seeps. In JUNOCC/ARTTRI/FESIDA, JUNOCC/ARTTRI/AGRSPI, and JUNOCC/bunchgrass communities.
physicalDescription: A small to medium sized perennial growing 7 1/2 inches to 2 feet tall (2-6 dm). The four-petalled lilac-purple blossoms with 1/2 inch long petals (1.2 cm) grow widely spaced on an elongated flower stalk. The hairless 1-2 inch long leaves (2-5 cm) have a bluish cast; those at the base have short stalks, the rest are stalkless and clasp the stems. Fruit is a skinny pod 1-2 inches long (3-4.5 cm) and curved upward.
ecologyComments: Occurs in areas with seasonal water. It requires undisturbed habitat (since it is readily eaten by cattle), but needs open but moist microsites, which is why it usually occurs in bare soils found under junipers or along stream washes.
globalRangeComments: Thelypodium eucosmum is limited to the United States, endemic to north-central Oregon. It occurs in the lower canyons of the Blue Mountains and along the tributaries of the John Day River in north-central, Oregon (Guerrant 2008).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

county: Croo, Desc, Gran, Harn, Klam, Lake
globalRangeComments: Historically known from northern California, eastern and central Oregon, and possibly from Yakima County, Washington. The only recently observed populations of var. howellii are located in northeastern California and Klamath County, Oregon.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Occurs in moist, alkaline valley bottoms, dominated by basin wildrye, alkali-grasses (Distichlis stricta, Puccinella lemmonii, Poa juncifolia), and black greasewood. Sites are usually in alluvial outwash areas, near streams or rivers, with seasonal moisture.
physicalDescription: Tallish (0.1-.8 m high), biennial to short lived perennial (occasionally blooming the first year), usually branched, with obvious, clasping (auriculate) stem leaves and large, bright pink-purple flowers (spathulate petals about 1 cm long).
ecologyComments: Most sites are located in areas adjacent to moderately high frequency floodplains - and may require some disturbance or open soils for good reproduction. The species is weedy in nature, and does well following some disturbance, although agriculture and heavy grazing will rapidly destroy populations.
globalRangeComments: Thelypodium howellii ssp. spectabilis only occurs in the United States. It is endemic to the northeastern corner of Oregon, occurring in the Baker-Powder River valley in Baker and Union Counties (NatureServe Network Database as of March 2021, USFWS 1999). As of 2021 the range is about 90 square kilometers (NatureServe Network Database as of March 2021).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: USA, sw OR, Josephine Co., Siskiyou Mts.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits low elevation ponds or sloughs, submersed or partially floating on the surface of slow moving water. Seasonal pools in Fraxinus latifolia woodland is one known locality in Clark County, WA. Associated species include Spiraea douglasii, Callitriche heterophylla, Fontinalis antipyretica, Ranunculus aquatilis, and Veronica spp. Absent from pools with introduced carp. Carp muddy water and eat all aquatic vegetation.
physicalDescription: Water Howellia is a glabrous, much-branched, annual, aquatic herb with fragile, submerged and floating stems that are up to 100 cm tall. The simple, alternate or occasionally opposite or whorled stem leaves are narrowly linear, 1-5 cm long, and entire-margined. Beneath the surface of the water, small flowers that produce seeds without opening are solitary in the leaf axils. Once the stems reach the surface, small, white flowers are borne in a narrow, terminal, leafy-bracted inflorescence. The white corolla is 2-3 mm long. Flowering occurs on the surface of the water. The fruit, which forms below the attachment of the petals, is a capsule that is 1-2 cm long containing elongate seeds that are up to 2-4 mm long.
globalRangeComments: Howellia aquatilis is a Pacific Northwest endemic known from northern California (Mendocino County), western Oregon, Washington, northern Idaho, and western Montana (Mincemoyer 2005). Extant populations are mostly clustered in three main population centers, one in Pierce County in western Washington, one in Spokane County in eastern Washington, and one in the Swan Valley in western Montana (Mincemoyer 2005).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: In Oregon, reported growing in the water of the Metolius River. Other states and province find it growing in fine-sand and silt shorelines of lakes and ponds; and in gently flowing water (has been reported to 1' deep). Associated species Washington include: Isoetes echinospora, Subularia aquatica, Tillaea erecta, Scirpus acutus, Eleocharis palustris, Potamogeton gramineus, P. epihydrous, P. richarsonii, P. illinoensis and P. natans. The Isoetes may be the best indicator although it too may be difficult to see (Buckingham 1986).
globalRangeComments: Coastal southwestern British Columbia (Douglas, 1989). Scattered in Washington, King County north to Whatcom County, and Clallam County (Washington Natural Heritage Program, 1981). Newfoundland to New Jersey, west to Minnesota; also on the Pacific coast and in Europe (Gleason, 1991).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Nemacladus capillaris is endemic to the western United States in California and southwestern Oregon (Jackson County), in the Coast Ranges, western Sierra Nevada, Cascade Range, and Modoc Plateau (Morin and Ayers 2020, Jepson Flora Project 2026). physicalDescription: A small hairy matted perennial growing 6 to 10 inches tall (15 to 25 cm) with flowers the color of apple blossoms (white tinged pink).  Petals are 1/2 to 3/4 inch long (1.3-2 cm); flowers grow 1 to 7 per stem.  The calyx is long and balloon like. Narrow leaves grow mainly matted at the base but also along the stems in 1 to 8 pairs.  Fruit is a narrow capsule.

habitatDescription: Inhabits undisturbed prairie on loessal hills, at low to mid elevations. Occassionally found in sagebrush scabland or open woodland. Associated species: Crataegus douglasii, Symphoricarpos albus & Festuca idahoensis. In Oregon, most sites are east or northeast slopes, in the Festuca idahoensis-Koeleria nidita plant association. The largest populations, however, occur on the Wallowa Lake terminal and lateral moraines in various aspects, and in an unusual habitat dominated by Artemisa ludiviciana and Festuca idahoensis.
physicalDescription: Spalding's Campion is a perennial with a simple or branched rootcrown. There are 4-7 pairs of sessile, broadly lance-shaped leaves that are 6-7 cm long below and gradually reduced in size upward. Herbage is long-hairy and very sticky. There are few to many flowers in a leafy, somewhat open inflorescence. The tubular calyx is ca. 15 mm long, has 10 nerves on its surface, and is very sticky. The corolla has 5 separate, white petals, each composed of a narrow claw that is ca. 15 mm long expanding into a broadened blade above. Only the entire or shallowly-lobed blade with 4 tiny wings at the base protrudes beyond the mouth of the calyx. The fruit is a capsule that is 10-15 mm long and filled with numerous tiny seeds.
ecologyComments: Occurs in climax grasslands in Wallowa County.
globalRangeComments: Silene spaldingii occurs in western North America as a regional endemic of eastern Washington, northeastern Oregon, northern Idaho, western Montana in the United States, and extending into southern British Columbia, Canada (USFWS 2007). In the United States it occurs in five physiographical regions: the Poulouse Prairie grasslands of Idaho and Washington, the Channeled Scablands of eastern Washington, the Blue Mountain Basins in Oregon, the Canyon Grasslands of the Snake River and its tributaries, and the Intermontane Valleys of Montana. Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1994 and 2025 (RARECAT 2024, NatureServe 2025, SEINet 2025).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Callitriche marginata occurs in western North America, from southwestern British Columbia in Canada, to Oregon, Idaho, California, and northern Baja California, Mexico. The range extent was estimated to be 870,000 square kilometers using herbarium specimens and photo-based observations documented between 1992 and 2023 (CCH2 Portal 2023, Flora of North America Editorial Committee 2019, GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023, Villaseñor 2016).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Sedum laxum ssp. heckneri is known from northwest California and southwest Oregon (Zika et al. 20180, Jepson Flora Project 2023, Oregon State University 2023). Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens, NatureServe Network occurrence data, and photo-based observations, collected between 1992 and 2023 (CCH2 Portal 2023, GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023, NatureServe 2023).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits serpentine outcrops on west or southwest slopes. Reported associated species are Rhus diversiloba, Achillea millefolium, Pityrogramma triangularis, Monardella odoratissima, Selaginella wallacei and several mosses.
physicalDescription: Succulent perennial herb with a greenish to reddish-purple stem whose top portion is densely glandular, 15-33 cm tall from a stout rootstock. Basal leaves flat spoon-shaped in a dense rosette. Stem leaves alternate and oblong. Petals yellow to greenish-yellow, 12-15 mm long, with stamens equaling to slightly longer than the calyx.
globalRangeComments: Sedum moranii is endemic to southwestern Oregon, along the lower Rogue River, in Josephine County (Meinke 1982, Zika et al. 2018). Populations are known from 2 km of the river corridor (Zika et al. 2018).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits sunny, dry slopes with good drainage. It has been found on a variety oftype of bedrock exposures: including diroite, granite, pyllite-schist, metavolcanics, metasedimentary, and ultramafics such as serpentine, soapstone and peridotite.Associated species: Sedum radiatum, Pinus ponderosa, and Arctostaphylos nevadensis.
globalRangeComments: This species is limited to the Applegate and Little Applegate River drainages of Jackson County, Oregon and Siskiyou County, California with one lone site barely in the Klamath River basin in California. About six populations are known from Siskiyou County, California. Total range for this species is about 20 x 17 miles.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.
Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Occurring in sparse forest or shrub comminities with A. canescens, often on southern exposures. Ranging from low elevations to ca. 1100 m.
ecologyComments: Many species of Arctostaphylos are stimulated by burning. The specific affect of fire on A. hispidula are not presently known.
globalRangeComments: Its range is limited to the Siskiyou region of SW Oregon, Curry County, and adjacent California.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

physicalDescription: Perennial, evergreen, multi-stemmed shrub that may be erect or trailing/matted. Stems have peeling reddish-gray bark. Leaves are oval to egg-shaped, dark green and shiny with golden crystalline glands on their undersides. There are 4-7 flowers per stem; flowers are reddish-purple to bright pink, fragrant, relatively large (16-28 mm), urn or bell-shaped (lacking a defined throat) to nearly flat as the petal lobes bend back. 10 stamens protrude conspicuously from each fully-open flower and have dense yellow hairs at their bases. Fruits are dry capsules that split open to release many tiny seeds. Flowers April to June and disperses seeds later in the summer (Amsberry et al. 2007, Oregon Flora Project 2007).
ecologyComments: Grows on rock outcrops within forests dominated by Pseudotsuga menziensii and Pinus lambertiana, sometimes Tsuga heterophylla stands. Dominant shrubs are Gaultheria shallon, Berberis nervosa, and Rhododendron macrophyllum. Rock substrate is silicified quartz; forest soil is of metavolcanic origin. Species may be limited to the rock outcrops due to low competition. Predators and parasites do not appear to be a threat or limit its distribution. Species is distylous though there does not appear to be any difference in pollen size.
globalRangeComments: Kalmiopsis fragrans is endemic to a narrow band of rocky habitat along the west slope of the southern Cascade Mountains within the North Umpqua River watershed in Douglas County, southwestern Oregon, USA (Meinke and Kaye 2007). Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1993 and 2024 (iNaturalist 2024, NatureServe 2024, OBIC 2024, OSU 2024, SEINet 2024).
references: Meinke, R. J. and T. N. Kaye.  2007.  Kalmiopsis fragrans (Ericaceae), a new distylous species from the southern Cascade mountains of Oregon.  Journal of the Botanical Research Institute of Texas 1(1): 9-19.

globalRangeComments: Vaccinium oxycoccos is a widespread circumboreal species, occurring in North America, Greenland, St. Pierre and Miquelon, northern Europe, and northern Asia (FNA 2009). In North America, it occurs throughout Canada and Alaska and Maine south to Maryland, west to Illinois and Minnesota, and in the western United States. Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens and photo-based observations collected between 1993 and 2024 (GBIF 2024, iNaturalist 2024, SEINet 2024).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Southern Harvey and Malheur Cos., Oregon, and Humbolt Co., Nevada, possibly in adjacent Owyhee Co., Idaho.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Occurs in meadows and moist ground along wayside ditches and along the Klamath River at ca. 1250 m. Primarily in grasslands dominated by Puccinella lemmonii and Poa juncifolia, with Chrysothamnus nauseosus usually present. Alfalfa and other weeds also common.
physicalDescription: Astragalus applegatei is a low lying perennial, herbaceous plant with slender stems appearing clustered or loosely spreading from a taproot. Mature plants may grow as a circular mat with a radius of 1-3 feet (1/3 - 1 m). Flowers are pea-like, light purple, about 1/4 inch (.6 cm) long with the lower petal almost pependicular to the flower stalk. Seed pods are about 1/3-1/2 inch (.8 - 1.25 cm) long with purple mottling.
ecologyComments: Alluvial flats, probably maintained by flooding of the Klamath River before the dams and dikes. Most habitat has been converted to agriculture.
globalRangeComments: Astragalus applegatei occurs in the western United States and is only found in the Lower Klamath Basin, near the city of Klamath Falls, in Klamath County, Oregon. Barneby (1964) suggested that the plant may also occur in adjacent Siskiyou County, California, but it has never been reported from California. Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1993 and 2024 (OSU 2024, NatureServe 2024).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Among sagebrush on stony flats and dry hillsides. Has also been observed in grassy meadows where individuals are more robust.
globalRangeComments: Astragalus atratus var. owyheensis is found from near Baker City, Oregon southeast to Owyhee and Twin Falls counties, Idaho and the headwaters of Humboldt River in Elko County, Nevada (Barneby 1989, FNA 2023). Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1993 and 2024 (SEINet 2024, OSU 2024, CPNWH 2024, NatureServe 2024).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Upper Sacramento Valley and west edge of the Klamath Basin, Shasta and Siskiyou Counties, California (Munz 1959). Peck (1961) reports southern Jackson County, Oregon to California.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Dry, open barrens. Can also occur in subalpine areas and fell-fields but not in this state.
globalRangeComments: Astragalus calycosus occurs in the western United States, from the Great Basin and Range of California, eastern Oregon, and Nevada, through southern Idaho, Utah, southwestern Wyoming, southwestern Colorado, northwestern and central New Mexico, and Arizona. The range extent is estimated to be 850,000 square kilometers, using herbarium specimen and photo-based observation data collected between 1992 and 2023 (Barneby 1989, GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Occurring on dry slopes, in areas with loess deposits, occasionally with sandy or rocky substrates, usually in the bluebunch wheatgrass-Idaho fescue (Agropyron spicatum-Festuca idahoensis) palouse grassland or canyon communities. The majority of sites are in roadsides adjacent to wheatlands, or on canyons above the streams and below the farmlands. Associcated species: Agropyron spicatum, Poa sandbergii, Festuca idahoensis, Bromus tectorum, Achillea millifolium, Phlox longifolia.
physicalDescription: A perennial herb that branches freely into small leaflets. The flowers consist of cream or yellowish petals emerging from a pouchlike base. The pods are pendulous and bear short, shaggy hairs.
ecologyComments: So much of the habitat of this species has been destroyed, that it is impossible to determine its ecological requirements.
globalRangeComments: North central Oregon, about the headwaters of Rock, Willow & Butler Creeks in Morrow Co., Thirty-mile Cr. in southeast Gilliam Co. & in the lower Umatilla Valley. in nw Umatilla Co. Generalized range of extant sites is 2000 sq. km., including historical collections another 1000 sq. km.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Astragalus conjunctus var. rickardii occurs in the Northwestern United States where it is endemic to the Columbia Plateau of north-central Oregon (Wasco County) and south-central Washington (Benton County) (Beck and Caplow 2006, Myers et al. 2020). Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data documented between 1983 and 2024 (CPNH, 2024, GBIF 2024, iNaturalist 2024, NatureServe 2024, SEINet 2024).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1999. A synonymized checklist and atlas with biological attributes for the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. First edition. In: Kartesz, J.T., and C.A. Meacham. Synthesis of the North American Flora, Version 1.0. North Carolina Botanical Garden, Chapel Hill, N.C.

habitatDescription: Occurs on open ash deposits, appearing as clayey bluffs in the canyonlands of the Owyhee Uplands. These knolls are nearly bare of other vegetation.  Associated with: Artemisia tridentata, Atriplex confertifolia, Salvia dorrii, Eriogonum ovalifolium, E. novonudum, Monardella odoratissima, Cryptantha interrupta, C. propria, Chaenactis douglasii, Eriophyllum lanatum, Caulanthus pilosus, and Astragalus eremiticus. Bromus tectorum or Agropyron spicatum often present.
physicalDescription: A small, wiry, perennial herb with one to three 2 to 6 inch tall (6-16cm) stems arising from an underground rootstock. Flowers are white, fade to yellow, are loosely clustered, grow on an upward curving stem and average 2 to 5 per bloom stalk. Leaves are wiry looking with 6 to 8 widely spaced tiny 1/4 inch leaflets on a stiff 1 to 3 1/2 inch (2-9cm) leaf stalk. Inflated fruit pods to 1inch long (2-2.5cm) hang down and are purple mottled on pale green.
ecologyComments: Usually in open, barren ash deposits which have not weathered to clay. Rarely produces many flowers or fruit, and often reproduces rhizomatously, which is unusual in this genus.
globalRangeComments: The range of Astragalus cusickii var. sterilis centers around a 30-mile stretch of the Owyhee River and side drainages in Malheur County, Oregon and adjacent Owyhee County, Idaho in the western United States. Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1993 and 2024 (CPNWH 2024, iNaturalist 2024, NatureServe 2024, SEINet 2024).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Ranges from very open, bare shallow-soiled sites over basalt bedrock with little vegetation to relatively bare openings in JUNOCC or PINPON forests.
ecologyComments: In open, edaphic ash deposits on basalt by the river.
globalRangeComments: Known only from the South Fork John Day River drainage, Grant County, Oregon, from about 3 miles south of its confluence with the main stem John Day River to about 20 miles upstream. All but one of the occurrences are within the same 7-mile stretch of river, clustering around the river from Jackass and Youngs Creek downstream. Historically reported from Klickitat County, Washington but considered extirpated from Washington.
references: Meyers, S.C., T. Jaster, K.E. Mitchell, T. Harvey, and L.K. Hardison, editors. 2020. Flora of Oregon. Volume 2: Dicots A-F. Botanical Research Institute of Texas, Fort Worth, TX. 861 pp.

globalRangeComments: Astragalus gambelianus occurs in western North America, in Baja California, California, extending north into southern Oregon. Range extent was estimated to be 370,000 square kilometers using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1992 and 2023 (CCH2 Portal 2023, GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023, NatureServe 2023, Villaseñor 2016).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Occuring on dry hillsides in gravelly or rocky soils, usually at high altitudes below 180 m, in "bunchgrass rangeland".
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Occuring on old river deposits, sandy places near rivers, sandy bluffs, and dunelike talus in the foothills. Assoc. species: Penstemon acuminata, Artemisia tridentata, Stipa comata, Oryzopsis hymenoides.
physicalDescription: Perennial herb, about 10 - 30 cm (4"-12") tall, slender and diffuse. Leaflets (15-25), paired except for the single terminal leaflet, together measuring about 4-11 cm (1 1/2" to 4 1/3") long. Flowers, 5-20, pea-like, and whitish. The fruits are peapod-like, 1 - 1.5 cm (3/8"-5/8") long, pendulous, with 10-16 seeds.
ecologyComments: Perennial herb occuring in steppe, shrub-steppe and desert shrub communities. Most inhabited sites are apparently fairly level to moderate in slope. The taxon grows in sandy soils particularly along old river deposits.
globalRangeComments: Mulford's Milkvetch only occurs in the northwestern United States, it is endemic to the western Snake River Plain in southwestern Idaho and adjacent eastern Oregon. It occurs from the Owyhee Uplands in Malheur County in Oregon, east to the Owyhee Front and Boise Foothills in Idaho, in Ada, Owyhee and Washington Counties (Mancuso 1999, NatureServe Network Database as of April 2021, Oregon Department of Agriculture 2014).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Occurring in very dry sites, on loose, sandy soil or pumice. Often found in/along dry water courses, in sagebrush or rabbitbrush openings in lodgepole pine forests (in the south) or in western Juniper woodlands (in the north), occ. on barren flats. Assoc. shrubs: Purshia tridentata, Artemisia tridentata, Chrysothamnus viscidiflorus; Others: Stipa occidentalis, Festuca idahoensis, Mimulus nanus, Penstemon humilus, and Leptodactylon pugens.
physicalDescription: A silvery hairy perennial herb, about 4"-12" long, branches spreading or prostrate from a short woody base. Leaves about 1 3/16"-1 9/16" long, comprised of 8-12 paired leaflets, each 1/8"-1/4" long, attached to a center rachis that persists and becomes hard and spin-like. The pale yellow pea-like flowers, about 1/8" long are few and loosely arranged on a single stalk which is equal to or longer than the leaves. Fruits are peapod-like, 3/16"-1/4" long, compressed, and densely hairy.
ecologyComments: Occurs in deep, loose, well drained soils. Many sites are old lake beds, probably filled with pumic or ash from Cascade mountain eruptions. Often in areas characterized by big sagebrush with western needlegrass, and often in frost pockets or lakebeds filled with volcanic ash, pumice or silts.
globalRangeComments: Astragalus peckii is endemic to central Oregon on the eastern foothills of the Cascades (Barneby 1964, Oregon Flora Project 2019). "The distribution of A. peckii is restricted to two counties and comprises a main population center, which covers a 64 sq km area, plus several naturally isolated populations located up to 200 km south of the population center" (Martin and Meinke 2012).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

physicalDescription: Broad-keeled milkvetch is a small perennial herb without prolonged stems; all leaves are clustered at the base of the plant on short branches of the rootcrown clothed with old leaf stalks. Pinnately compound leaves, 1-9 cm long, have 7-15 oblong to elliptic, often blunt-tipped leaflets. Foliage is sparsely covered with gray or silver hairs. Spreading flower stalks arise from amongst the leaves and bear 3-9 flowers near the tip. Whitish, pea-like flowers are 6-9 mm long with an upper petal that is barely reflexed and nearly the same length as the others. The calyx is 3-5 mm long and sparsely covered with white or black hairs. Inflated, egg-shaped fruits are papery, purple-mottled, and 15-33 mm (ca. 1 in) long. Fruits that resemble small Chinese lanterns are usually found on the ground near the base of the plant.
globalRangeComments: Astragalus platytropis occurs in the western United States where it occurs from Montana and central Idaho, southward through Nevada to eastern California, and at the eastern edge of its range in western Wyoming. Range extent was estimated to be 450,000 square kilometers using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1994 and 2025 (RARECAT 2024, GBIF 2025, iNaturalist 2025, NatureServe 2025, SEINet 2025).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Occurring on brushy stream banks & gravel bars from ca. 1280to 2150 m elevation. Sometimes subject to flooding, rarely found on open flats in the forest near streams. Assoc. species: Astragalus alpinus, Oxytropis viscida, Hedysarum boreale
globalRangeComments: Astragalus robbinsii var. alpiniformis grows only in the Wallowa Mountians of northeastern Oregon (FNA 2023). Range extent was estimated to 148 sq km using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1987 and 2024 (iNaturalist 2024, SEINet 2024, CPNWH 2024, NatureServe 2024).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Found in sagebrush openings, under Pinus ponderosa and on welded tuff rock outcrops in juniper/sagebrush. Also can be found in roadways and other disturbed areas. However, not as abundant as other plants which are capable of invading disturbed areas. Associated with: Artemisia tridentata, A. arbuscula, Pinus ponderosa, Juniperus occidentalis, Chrysothamnus nauseosus, C. viscidiflorus, Ribes viscosissimum, Sitanion hystrix, Epilobium paniculatum, Eriophyllum lanatum, Phacelia hastata, Senicio canus, Gilia congesta, Leptodactylon pungesn, Eriogonum ovalifolium, El umbellatum, Phlox sp., Antennaria sp., and Lupinus sp.
ecologyComments: This plant may be an early seral species within the pine forest community, appearing in openings made by fire.
globalRangeComments: Blue Mountain Milkvetch occurs in the northwestern United States, it is endemic to eastern Oregon, where it occurs in the Blue Mountains and Northern Basin and Range regions. Nearly all known locations are in Harney County and it also occurs in Crook County, Oregon. The range extent is estimated to be 4,600 square kilometers (NatureServe 2022, SEINet 2022).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Ocurring on dry, rocky soils often with a thin overlying sandy or silty layer. Inhabits pine and sagebrush transition areas, such as dry oak and dry oak-pine savannas, bitterbrush steppe and moist margin sagebrush communities, as well as along roadsides in the area. Associated species: Agropyron spicatum, Festuca idahoensis, Bromus tectorum, Astragalus purshii, Sanguisorba occidentalis, and Alyssum alyssoides.
physicalDescription: Astragalus tyghensis is a densely white hairy perennial herb with closely clustered stems 20 to 30 cm (8 to 12 inches) high. It has dense clusters of 20 to 40 flowers which are clear light yellow in color. The leaf stalks are 7 to 10 cm (3 to 4 inches) long; 15 to 25 oval leaflets grow along both sides of the stalks. The 0.6 cm (1/4 inch) fruit pod is densely white hairy and hangs down or is horizontal.
ecologyComments: Occurs in native grassland and sagebrush-canyon areas. Fires were formerly much more common, but do not appear to be critical for this species.
globalRangeComments: Astragalus tyghensis is endemic to Oregon, in the western United States, and known only from the Tygh Valley and near the Deschutes River in eastern Wasco County.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Dry open oak and pine woodlands, low to mid-elevation
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

county: Bent, Clac, Doug, Lane, Linn, Mari, Polk, Wash, Yamh
habitatDescription: Inhabits roadsides and fencerows in grassland or climbing in low scrubby vegetaion. Associated species: Quercus garryana, Holodiscus discolor, Rhus diversiloba, Aster hallii, Delphinium pavonaceum, and Vicia spp.
physicalDescription: A rhizomatous, climbing perennial herb, hairless or sparsely hairy, with stems 30-100 cm long. Leaves are compound with 6-12 egg- to ellipse-shaped, 2-5 cm x 0.7-3 cm leaflets and egg-shaped stipules that are generally one-fifth to one-half as long as the leaflets; leaves end in a tendril. There are 5 to 15, 13-17 mm long whitish flowers per stem that turn light brown or orange as they age. The banner petal of each flower is purplish-rose lined. Fruits are pods 3-5 cm long and 4-7 mm broad.
globalRangeComments: Occurs in the Willamette and Umpqua Valleys in western Oregon, ranging from Washington County south to Lane County. Also occurs somewhat disjunctly (approximately 125 km distant) in Lewis County, southwest Washington. Using GIS tools, range extent was estimated to be approximately 21,700 square km.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.
Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: This taxon occurs in the western United States from southeastern Oregon and California (FNA 2023, Jepson Flora Project 2026, OSU 2026). Range extent was estimated to be over 110,000 square kilometers using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data documented between 1994 and 2025 (RARECAT 2025, GBIF 2026, iNaturalist 2026, NatureServe 2026, SEINet 2026). See each of the varieties for more information.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits dry, granite outcrops at or near ridges and summitsat ca 2100-2300 m. Associated species: Horkelia hendersonii, Castilleja arachnoidea, Eriogonum spp., and Phlox sp.
physicalDescription: A perennial herb forming clumps 15-20 cm in diameter. When flowering, plants are 7-12 cm tall with sturdy upright to spreading flower stalks. Plants (except for upper leaf surfaces and flowers) are covered with dense woolly hairs. The silver-edged leaves are numerous, ascending, and crowded from the basal crown; they are palmately compound, with 5-7 leaflets each 1-2 cm long. Flower stalks produce a large dense spike 3.5-7 cm long of numerous blue-purple flowers; petals are about 11 mm long, with the banner (upper petal) reddish and smooth banner and the keel (lower petal) whitish with sparse hairs on its margin. Blooms in July and August.
globalRangeComments: Lupinus aridus ssp. ashlandensis is known only from the summit and high subalpine to alpine slopes on the western flank of Mount Ashland, part of the Siskiyou Range in southern Oregon (Jackson County) in the western United States.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Populations verified for five sites in eastern Baker County along the Burn River. Ssp. cusickii found within dry, open land extending from barren upper slopes to rather dense stand of Atremisia on lower slopes. Substrate mainly consist of eroding slopes of whitish volcanic ash.
ecologyComments: Lupinus cusickii are often associated with Ariemisia spp and Chrysothamnus spp, theydo not occur in abundance and thrive in dry soil composed volcanic ash.
globalRangeComments: Lupinus cusickii ssp. cusickii is known only from one small valley in the Blue Mountains in Baker County, Oregon, U.S.A. (Trowbridge et al. 2012). This taxon has been falsely reported from Idaho, Washington, Nevada, and Utah. Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1993 and 2024 (CPNWH 2024, NatureServe 2024, SEINet 2024).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Grasslands and open woodlands at low elevations in the Willamette and Umpqua Valleys. || Open grassy prairies and meadow edges often near oak. In Douglas County, this lupine also grows in Douglas fir and madrone woodlands.
physicalDescription: A bluish flowered perennial lupine 5-8 dm tall. Stems and petioles with mostly short hairs with some longer spreading hairs. Few stems, 9-11 leaflets, narrow , oblanceolate, hairless above and silky hairs below.
ecologyComments: Fire supression may be a factor in declines of this species. Larvae of a rare butterfly, Icaricia icarioides fenderi, Fender's blue butterfly, feeds on leaves and flowers of this lupine.
globalRangeComments: Known from Douglas County, Oregon, north to Lewis County, Washington. It previously occurred in southern British Columbia but has not been found there since the 1920’s. In Oregon, it occurs in the Willamette and Umpqua Valleys.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits low hillsides and flats on dry open sites in moderately stoney soil frequently along roadsides. Associated species: Artemisia tridentata, Agropyron cristatum, Bromus tectorum, and Lupinus caudatus.
ecologyComments: Seems to tolerate moderate disturbance.
globalRangeComments: Occurs in Harney and Malheur Counties, Oregon.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Occurring near melting snowbanks or other cool, damp sites, in coniferous forests at middle to upper elevations with Vaccinium spp.
globalRangeComments: Tracy's Lupine occurs in the northwestern United States, in the Klamath Mountains of northern California, and the Siskiyou Mountains of southwestern Oregon. The range extent is estimated to be 18,400 square kilometers, using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1991 and 2023 (CCH2 Portal 2023, Flora of North America Editorial Committee 2023, GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023, NatureServe 2023).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Oxytropis sericea var. sericea is known from southeastern Oregon, to southern Montana and South Dakota, south to Nevada, Utah, New Mexico, and Texas (Flora of North America Editorial Committee 2023). Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens collected between 1992 and 2023 (GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023, SEINet 2023).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits primarily south or west slopes, although is found widely on ridgetops, flats and all aspects except north exposures. Occurs at lower elevations, on ridges, slopes and flats above creeks.nages at lower elevations. Occurs in open forests, usually with some mixed conifer and hardwoods (primarily Quercus kelloggii), but can persist in closed canopy forests. However, it does best following disturbance, in open sites, not infrequently on clear cuts, within a mixed evergreen-oak woods habitat type. The substrate is primarily peridotite.
ecologyComments: This is a pioneer species, but rhizomatous with limited seed production. Fire or some kind of disturbance is necessary for reproduction.Isolated stems have been found in closed canopy forests which have not burned in 40 years.
globalRangeComments: Sophora leachiana is endemic to Josephine County, Oregon.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Occurs in northeast Oregon, southeast Washington, and adjacent Idaho (Isely 1998).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Occurs on barren tuffaceous hillsides, shaley crests and talus, and reddish ash-flow tuff. Reported associated species are: Purshia tridentata, Chrysothamnus nauseosus, Artemisia tridentata, Periphyllum, Phacelia, Lygodesmia spinosa, Eriogonum microthecum and Oryzopsis hymenoides.
ecologyComments: Populations tend to be local, limited by the limited eroded ash habitats.
globalRangeComments: Occurs in Nevada (Elko County) and Oregon (Harney and Malheur County).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits bleak slopes composed of loose diatomaceous talus or volcanic ash. Surrounding plant communities are dominated by sagebrush and juniper, with the few direct associates being annuals: Mimulus cusickii, Senecio ertterae, Mentzelia spp.
physicalDescription: Perennial, branching clover, up to 20 cm (8") tall, with rose colored flowers, corollas are 1.2-1.8 cm (1/2" to 3/4") long (Oregon Department of Agriculture 2014).
ecologyComments: Has large, fleshy spreading root system that allows for deep penetration into cracks.
globalRangeComments: Owyhee Clover occurs in the northwestern United States, it is endemic to a small area of the Owyhee Uplands, in Malheur County, in southeastern Oregon, and adjacent Owyhee County, Idaho. The range extent is estimated to be 738 square kilometers (iNaturalist 2022, NatureServe 2022, SEINet 2022).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Wet shady areas, along springs, seeps, streams, rivers and other waterways. Gravelly/cobbly to gravelly/sandy substrate. Growing in coniferous forests dominated by Pseudotsuga menziesii, Tsuga heterophylla, Thuja plicata, and Abies amabilis.
ecologyComments: Cold water may be a requirement though this has not been proven
globalRangeComments: The taxon is restricted to the western Cascades of  Lane, Marion, Linn, Clackamas and Multnomah Counties in Oregon and Skamania and Clark Counties, Washington.  Most of the Oregon occurrences are found in Clackamas County, with the other 4 counties having 1 or 2 populations each.

habitatDescription: Inhabits gravelly hillsides to loam soils in open woods, occasionally along banks of streams, at 600 to 1200 m. It is restricted to serpentine substrates with little associated vegetation.

globalRangeComments: Dicentra pauciflora occurs in the western United States, mainly in the Sierra Nevada of California and also in Western Transverse Ranges of southern California, the Klamath Range, and Cascade Range of northern California and southwestern Oregon. Range extent was estimated to be 131,400 square kilometers, using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1992 and 2023 (CCH2 2023, FNA 1997, GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023, Jepson Flora Project 2023, NatureServe 2023, SEINet 2023).

habitatDescription: Inhabits mid to upper elevation of Abies dominated forests. The Cascade populations are in relatively cool, mesic sites which experience significant winter snow accumulation. It may be found as an understory herb in open forested stands and as a principal component in herb dominated meadows. Assoc: Xerophyllum tenax, Trifolium howellii, Rudbeckia occidentalis, Pteridium aquilinum, Festuca californica.
ecologyComments: Population size appears to be larger in the central part of its range at the Rogue-Umpqua Divide.
globalRangeComments: Frasera umpquensis occurs in the central-western portion of the Cascades Mountains of Oregon, with some isolated stations in the Klamath Mountains of southern Oregon and northern California. The most northern populations are in Lane County, Oregon and the most southern in California in the Shasta-Trinity National Forest. Most of the populations are centered around the divide between the Rogue and Umpqua rivers in Douglas and Jackson counties, Oregon.
references: Wilson, B.L., V. Hipkins, and T.N. Kaye. 2010. One taxon or two: are Frasera umpquaensis and F. fastigiata (Gentianaceae) distinct species?. Madroño, 57(2): 106-119.

habitatDescription: Restricted to serpentine bogs and marshes at elevations from ca. 140 to 1000 m. Assoc. species: Darlingtonia californica, Hastingsia bracteosa, Lilium pardalinum, Rudbeckia californica, Rhododendron occidentale & Cypripedium californica
globalRangeComments: Known only from the Siskiyou Mountains of southwestern Oregon and extreme northern California (Josephine and Curry Counties, Oregon and Del Norte County, California) and one disjunct population at Red Mountain in Mendocino County, California (Kagan et al. 2006).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Occurs in Oregon and California (Del Norte, Humboldt, Siskiyou and Trinity Counties).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

physicalDescription: Slender Gentian is a small, glabrous, annual herb which stands 2-15 cm tall; Montana collections are on the small end of this range. The stems are 4-angled and may be branched; those of small plants are often unbranched. There are usually several spoon-shaped basal leaves which are 3-10 mm long, and few, if any, slightly larger, opposite stem leaves, which are 5-15 mm long. There are one to a few flowers per stem borne singly on long pedicels; stems of small plants are often reduced to single, flowered, leafless scapes. The flowers have 4 green sepals which are about half as long as the corolla. The white to bluish-purple corolla is 8-15 mm long and is tubular-shaped with 4 terminal lobes which are about one-third as long as the tube; the inner surface of each lobe has two fringed scales near its base. There are 4 stamens attached to the inside of the corolla tube and a single basal pistil.
globalRangeComments: Circumboreal, south in N. America to Que., NM, and CA. Sparse.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits sandy beach dunes and bluffs near the coast. In partially stabilized dunes with Baccharis pilularia, Fragaria chilensis, Polygonum paronychia, Franseia chamissonis, and Abronia latifoia. Also in unstabilized dunes with Lupinus littoralis, Artemisia pycnocephala, and Abronia latifolia.
physicalDescription: Perennial, evergreen herb with many branching stems from a flattened mat. Typically, the stems are decumbent, meaning lying or trailing on the ground with the end tending to climb. The foliage has a silvery appearance from many short appressed hairs on the leaves. The 1 to 2 inch leaves are either entire or may have two basal lobes. The surface of the leaves is deeply impressed with veins. The white flowers are in scorpioid cymes (or rounded heads) at the tip of stems. One to many cymes make up each flowering head. The five stamens are exerted. Flowers are present May through August. Fruits are produced from June through August.
ecologyComments: Occurs in open sand and partially stabilized dunes. Threatened by secondary succession, from natural and artifical causes.
globalRangeComments: Phacelia argentea occurs only in the northwestern United States, in southwestern Oregon along the Pacific coast of Coos and Curry counties, and in adjacent northern California, along the coast in Del Norte County, as far south as Crescent City (Kalt 2008, NatureServe Network Database as of March 2021, Oregon Department of Agriculture 2014).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Phacelia minutissima occurs in the northwestern United States, in mountainous areas of northern Nevada, eastern Oregon, southwestern Idaho and central Washington. The range extent is estimated to be 135,000 square kilometers (NatureServe 2022, SEINet 2022).

habitatDescription: Inhabits shallow soils of steep banks or hillsides to nearly 1300 m, preferring open faces, usually moist or seeping in the spring and surrounded by open woodland. Assoc: moss or Salaginella, Trifolium sp, Mimulus, Micropus sp, Eriogonum
globalRangeComments: Restricted to the Umpqua Valley and upper Middle Fork of the Coquille River drainages of Douglas and Coos Counties, Oregon. Two outlying populations in adjacent drainages in Lane and Josephine Counties.

habitatDescription: Shallow soils on, seasonally wet at lower to mid-elevations in mixed conifer community. Associated species include: Mimulus guttatus, M. pulsiferae, Trifolium sp., Plectritis congesta, Floerkea proserpinacoides, Saxifraga howellii, moss. sometimes Romanzoffia californica
globalRangeComments: Romanzoffia thompsonii is endemic to the central and southern Cascade and Siskiyou Mountains in to western Oregon in the northwestern United States, predominantly in the foothills to mid-elevations (Marttala 1996, OSU 2025). Range extent was estimated to be approximately 15,000 square kilometers using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data documented between 1994 and 2025 (RARECAT 2024, GBIF 2025, iNaturalist 2025, NatureServe 2025, SEINet 2025).

habitatDescription: Found on dry slopes at mid to upper elevations, usually on loose, rocky substrate. Associated species include Artemisia spp., Penstemon spp., and Festuca spp.
physicalDescription: Cusick's Horse-mint is an herbaceous, long-lived perennial with numerous stems, woody at the base arising from a branched rootcrown surmounting a taproot. Plants are 1-2 dm high, but the stems often lie prostrate beneath the surface spreading from the rootcrown. Opposite leaves have blades that are 1-2 cm long and triangular with a rounded base and a petiole that is up to 1 cm long. Foliage is covered with fine, short hairs. White flowers are borne among purple-tipped bracts in a head-like inflorescence that is 1.5-4 cm long. The tubular corolla is 8-12 mm long, and the purple-tinged calyx is tubular with 5 pointed lobes. The 5 stamens are exserted from the mouth of the flower tube.
globalRangeComments: Agastache cusickii occurs in Oregon (Harney, Malheur, and Wheeler Counties), central Idaho, northern and central Nevada (Steens, Santa Rosa, White Pine, and Toiyabe Mountains), southwestern Montana in Beaverhead County, and possibly northeastern California in Siskiyou County. Reported from Butte, Clark, Custer, and Lemhi Counties in Idaho.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Pogogyne floribunda occurs in the Great Basin of the northwestern United States, in northeastern California, southern Oregon and southwestern Idaho. Most populations are in on the Modoc Plateau in Modoc, Lassen, and Shasta counties, California, with Siskiyou County having only one known population, in Lake and Klamath counties Oregon, and in Ada County, Idaho. Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1992 and 2023 (CCH2 Portal 2023, CNDDB 2023, GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023, Jokerst 1992, NatureServe 2023).

habitatDescription: Prefers vernal pool habitats and occurs also in shallow, rocky, clayey soil at elevations, on level sites at least partially shaded and moist in spring. Assoc. species: Pinus ponderosa, perennial grasses & annual forbs.
ecologyComments: Ofen found in recent basalt flows and other openings in the coniferous forests of the south Cascades.
globalRangeComments: Limnanthes floccosa ssp. bellingeriana occurs in Jackson and Lake Counties, Oregon and adjacent California in the western United States.

habitatDescription: Inhabits the periphery of vernal pools at ca 375-400 m, near the wetter, inner edges as opposed to the drier outer fringes like the sympatric ssp. floccosa. Assoc. species: Lupinus sp., Trifolium sp., Myosurus minimus & Baeria chrysostoma.
globalRangeComments: This annual plant only occurs in the United States, in southwestern Oregon. It is endemic to the Rogue River Valley in Jackson County, Oregon. Most populations centered in the Agate Desert region north of the city of Medford, Oregon. The entire range of known extant populations is less than 100 square km (40 square miles) in the Rogue River Valley (NatureServe Network Database as of March 2021).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits small depressions in thin clay soil overlying old basalt at the edges of deep vernal pools which dry by mid-summer, generally in full sun. Associated with Deschampsia danthoniodes, Alopecurus geniculatus, Baeria chrysostoma, Collinsia sp., & Lupinus sp., Plagiobothrys, and Isoetes bolanderi.
physicalDescription: A small (up to one dm tall) delicate annual with divided leaves and showy white flowers with yellow centers.
ecologyComments: The number of plants present is directly correlated with the rainfall and water present in the vernal pools.
globalRangeComments: This annual plant is known from the United States, and is endemic to southwestern Oregon. It only occurs on two mesas at Table Rock, in Jackson County, Oregon.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits rocky, alluvial flats, in serpentine areas, which are moist to wet in early spring. It is occasionally found in ditches or disturbed area, but the natural habitat is flat, aluvial plains, usually in open Pinus ponderosa - Quercus garryana valley bottomlands, with grasses (Danthonia californica, Deschampsia danthoides, Poa scrabrella, Agrostis microphylla). Often associated with Ceanothus cuneatus.
ecologyComments: Valley bottom species occuring in vernally moist areas, which is able to survive in some irrigation ditches and disturbed areas. Apparently requires some soil over serpentine substrate.
globalRangeComments: Limited to the southwestern corner of Oregon.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Edaphic endemic, found only on green or grey montmorillonite derived from the Succor Creek formation with abnormally high K content at ca 1400m. Associates: Cleomella macbrideana, Phacelia lutea, Monolepis pusilla, Cleome lutea, mentzilia alba, and often Chaenatis cuskin.
physicalDescription: A small, finely hairy, branching annual growing 2 to 4 1/2 inches tall (5-12 cm), with small bright yellow 1/3 inch long flowers clustered in a terminal head sitting upon 2 or 3 smallish leaf-like structures. Few toothed leaves are crowded below and are usually less hairy then the stems. The fruit is a 4-sided capsule.
ecologyComments: Over time, grasses and herbs may slowly colonize the ash, alter the soil composition and replace M. mollis. (Smithman, 1989)
globalRangeComments: The Smooth Stickleaf (Mentzelia mollis) occurs in the western United States, in the Great Basin of northwestern Nevada (Black Rock Desert), and in the Owyhee Desert of southeastern Oregon and nearby western Idaho. It is an edaphic endemic, restricted to volcanic ash outcrops in the Succor Creek drainage, Malheur County, Oregon, adjacent Idaho, plus one historic occurrence near Harper, Oregon (in Malheur County) and the disjunct occurrences in Nevada. The range extent is estimated to be 6400 square kilometers (Flora of North America Editorial Committee 2016, Glad 1975, Glad 1976, Mancuso et al. 2019, NatureServe 2023, Oregon Department of Agriculture 2014, SEINet 2023).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Restricted to volcanic ash high in K, growing on loose slopes devoid of woody vegetation within surrounding Artemisia-Atriplex/bunchgrass zones growing with other ash endemics such as Senecio ertterae, Trifolium owyheense, and Phacelia lutea.
physicalDescription: Small, upright annual forb with linear leaves, solitary yellow flowers in terminal clusters. Has five yellow petals 8-15 mm long, and triangular sepals. The capsules range from 15-30 mm long.
globalRangeComments: Mentzelia packardiae is a narrow endemic of the Leslie Gulch area in extreme east-central Malheur County, Oregon, near the Idaho border (Flora of North America Editorial Committee 2016). Most occurrences are within a 3-mile area.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

physicalDescription: Toothcup is a small, glabrous annual with simple or branched, erect to prostrate stems that are up to 10 cm high. The opposite, narrowly lance-shaped leaves have short petioles and are 15-30 mm long. The tiny, solitary flowers are sessile in the axils of upper leaves. The cup-shaped, shallowly 4-lobed calyx is 1-3 mm long in flower but up to 4 mm long in fruit. The 4 stamens are shorter than the 1 mm long, white petals. The fruit is a globose capsule that is ca. 3 mm across.
globalRangeComments: Rotala ramosior occurs in temperate and tropical North and South America, from southern British Columbia and Ontario in Canada, the United States, Mexico, Cental America and the Caribbean, to Peru and Brazil. It occurs in much of the eastern United States, from southern New England, to Florida, central Texas and the eastern Great Plains. It occurs in the Central Valley of California and at scattered locations elsewhere in the western United States. It is introduced in Africa, Europe and Asia. The native range extent in the Americas is estimated to be 34 million square kilometers (GBIF 2023, Godfrey and Wooten 1981, Graham 2022).
