physicalDescription: An herbaceous perennial with palmately lobed basal leaves, upper stem leaves deeply divided, and stems variably covered with simple hairs; plants have short, thick, twisted underground stems as well as a system of fine roots extending from a stout taproot. Plants produce numerous flowering stems 60 to 100 cm tall, each with 30 to 100 pink flowers on very short stalks. Mature plants produce either exclusively female flowers, or flowers with both male and female parts. Female flowers are generally smaller and lack functioning pollen sacs at the ends of the stamens. The stamens are fused at the base to form a tube around the style. Fruits consist of a ring of 7 to 9 single-seeded, beaked segments (like segments of an orange), which separate at maturity (USFWS 1998).
ecologyComments: Appears to tolerate minor disturbance. Secondary succession is a major threat to the natural grasslands in the Willamette Valley. Oregon ash canopy is invading these habitats.
globalRangeComments: Most sites occur in the Willamette Valley of Oregon, from southern Benton County northward through the central and western Willamette Valley to central Washington County, Oregon (USFWS 2010). Also found at several higher elevation meadows in the northern Coast Range of Oregon that flank the western Willamette Valley in Yamhill, Washington, Tillamook, counties, Oregon (USFWS 2010). Two other populations are known from the Puget Trough of adjacent southwest Washington, in Cowlitz and Lewis counties, Washington (Camp and Gamon 2011).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Sweet Bayberry (Myrica gale) has a circumboreal distribution, it occurs in North America, western and northern Europe, and northeast Asia. Range extent was estimated to be 30 million square kilometers using herbarium specimens and photo-based observations documented between 1993 and 2024 (FNA 1997, GBIF 2024, iNaturalist 2024, POWO 2024).

physicalDescription: Mirabilis macfarlanei is a perennial forb with a stout, deep-seated taproot, and freely branched, decumbent or ascending stems forming small to large clumps. Leaves are opposite, somewhat succulent, green above, and glaucescent below. The lower leaves are orbicular or ovate-deltoid in shape, becoming progressively smaller towards the tip of the stem. The inflorescence is comprised of a cluster of 4-7 flowers subtended by an involucre. The striking, 5-merous, bright magenta-colored flowers are up to 25 mm long and 25 mm wide. They are funnel-form shaped with a widely expanding limb and exerted stamens.
ecologyComments: It may be affected by a fungal infection and insect predation. Extensive searches have located only four populations, most which have few plants.

habitatDescription: Open areas, flat to gently sloping ridges at mid-elevations in the cold desert environment of Owyhee uplands. Substrate is a barren, shallow, gravelly to rocky soil overlying basalt or rhyolite flows. Sites generally shrubless but associated with herbaceous species, such as Lewisia rediviva, Sitanion hystrix, Poa sandbergii, Lomatium spp., Eriogonum spp., Phlox spp., Penstemon deustus, Allium cf. parvum, Phoenicaulis cheiranthoides, and Erigeron spp. Common shrubs in the vicinity are Artemisia arbuscula, Chrysothamnus nauseosus, and Purshia tridentata. Aspects include N, S and SW. Artemisia arbuscula-Poa sandbergii lithosolic association.
physicalDescription: A perennial herb forming mats up to 2 dm across and about 1 dm high, including the flowering stalk. The plants have a branched woody base and produce silvery-gray narrow leaves about 2 cm long. Flowers are pale to bright yellow, which may become tinged with red as they age. They are borne on leafless stems, and are tightly grouped in ball-like clusters up to 2 cm across. Individual flowers are small, less than 3 mm, with 6 petals each. Fruits form within the flowers and are inconspicuous and seed-like (Wright 1989).
ecologyComments: Barren, shallow soils, desert areas. Gravelly to rocky soil overlying basalt and rhyolite flows substrates. Covers <1% at known sites. Apparently colonizes rocky barren areas. Able to withstand minor disturbance; evidenced by frost action and pedestalling.

globalRangeComments: Lewisia columbiana var. columbiana occurs in western North America from British Columbia, Canada south to Oregon and Washington in the United States (FNA 2003). This taxon was also reported in Idaho (Kartesz 1996), from a single locality in Bonner County (Steele et. al. 1981), but its current status in the state is unknown (INHP 2002). Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1994 and 2025 (RARECAT 2024, CPNWH 2025, iNaturalist 2025, NatureServe 2025).

habitatDescription: On Onion Peak it occurs at the summit on moist soils at the edge of Cladothamnus scrub and in rock crevices on the shaded north slope under forest remnants of Abies amabilis and Tsuga heterophylla. At Saddle Mountain it associates with Synthyris schizantha and Saxifraga occidentalis on seasonally moist north-facing slopes near the summit. In Tillamook County it occurs in mats of moss on the hard basalt bank of the Trask River with Mimulus guttatus, Saxifraga nuttallii, Acer, and Alnus. ||Wet seepy areas, open or shaded, from high rocky peaks to edges of river banks.
physicalDescription: A perennial herb up to 45 cm tall. Flowers have five lavender to magenta petals, attached to a white corolla tube with a thin, wavy, reddish to purplish line at the base. Stamens are maroon to dark purple and their filaments are not united at the base. Tip of stigma is not enlarged. Fruit is a capsule with an operculum, a cap-like structure that pops off when seeds are ready for dispersal. Leaves are in a basal rosettes and are oval to elliptical in shape; leaf margins are often toothed, but may also be smooth. Flowering April-July.
globalRangeComments: Restricted to the Coast Ranges of northwestern Oregon and southwestern Washington; occurs at scattered sites from the southern Olympic mountains, WA (Mt. Colonel Bob) to Tillamook County, OR (including Saddle Mountain and Onion Peak, Clatsop Co., OR) (Chambers 2006). Chambers (2006) hypothesized that low-elevation populations along rivers in Tillamook Co. may have become established by seeds washed down from the mountain populations.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1999. A synonymized checklist and atlas with biological attributes for the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. First edition. In: Kartesz, J.T., and C.A. Meacham. Synthesis of the North American Flora, Version 1.0. North Carolina Botanical Garden, Chapel Hill, N.C.

habitatDescription: Inhabits dry roadside ditches and cliffs, moist rocky slopes and lowland meadows, dirt at cliff bases, and, and especially rocky (basaltic) ledges. The plant seems to grow in undisturbed sites, at elevations from 125 to 200 feet. Associated species include shrubby genera like: Holodiscus, Philadelphus, Symphoricarpos, Rhus, and Quercus. Openings in or edges of oak woodlands, also on cliffs and rocky areas.
physicalDescription: A slender perennial delphinium, 8 to 23 1/2 inches tall (20 to 60 cm).  White to cream colored flowers grow in an elongated cluster of 6 to 30 individuals. The upper petals are tipped with blue or lavender and the lower petals are sometimes bluish tinged.  Leaves are 1  to 2 1/2 inches wide (3 to 6 cm) and are divided into narrow finger-like divisions.
globalRangeComments: Northern Willamette Valley, Oregon, in Clackamas, Marion, Washington, and Multnomah counties. One small disjunct population in Lewis County, Washington. Generalized range in Oregon is 1800 sq. km. and with the inclusion of the Washington population, it's estimated to triple that number.

physicalDescription: This white flowered delphinium is a perennial. It grows 1 to 3 feet tall (3-9 dm). Several to many flowers grow along the bloom stalk. The true upper petals are dark blue and the lower petals are faintly tinged blue. Leaves grow mainly along the stem and measure up to 8 1/2 inches long (22 cm) with stalk near bottom of plant to much smaller above. They are deeply cut.
ecologyComments: Occurs in Willamette Valley prairies, which have been maintained as prairies by fires, set by native Indians. Without fires, the habitat will become forested.
globalRangeComments: Known only from 5 counties in the Willamette Valley of Oregon with most of the populations in Benton and Polk counties.

The microhabitat in Oregon is the tops of exposed basalt bluffs, in a Agropyron spicatum-Festuca idahoensis grassland. In Oregon it is associated more with Oak and Ponderosa pine than in Washington. || Oak woodlands; crevices on rocky outcrops in mixed woodlands of oak, Douglas fir and pine.
physicalDescription: A compact perennial buttercup 2 to 7 in (5 to 20 cm) tall with finely dissected leaves and 1 or several bright yellow flowers on a 3 to 6 in (8 to 15 cm) stem. Nectary scale is unfringed usually.
ecologyComments: The habitat of this species is in an area with a fairly high natural fire frequency. Fire supression has reduced fires, and altered this habitat, although its microsites in Oregon probably protect it from fires.
globalRangeComments: Obscure Buttercup (Ranunculus triternatus) occurs in western North America, only in the Pacific Northwest of the United States, in the Columbia Hills of Klickitat County in southern Washington and nearby Mill Creek drainage in Hood River County and Wasco County, northern Oregon. It does not occur in Idaho or Nevada. Range extent was estimated to be about 344 square kilometers, using herbarium specimens and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1994 and 2025 (GBIF 2025, Giblin et al. 2024, NatureServe 2025, RARECAT 2024, SEINet 2025, Tiehm and Lucero 2024, WNHP 2025).

physicalDescription: Alpine Meadowrue is a small, perennial herb with mostly simple and nearly leafless stems that are 3-18 cm tall and arising from extensive, slender rhizomes. Each leaf has a slender petiole and is twice-pinnately divided into broad, 3-lobed segments that are 3-8 mm long. Herbage is glabrous or occasionally glandular and covered with a thin, bluish wax. The flowers have both anthers and pistils and are borne on short, nodding stalks in a narrow, terminal inflorescence. The 5 small sepals are purplish and fall soon after opening; petals are lacking. The 2-4 achenes are narrowly elliptic in outline, 2-4 mm long, and prominently ribbed.
globalRangeComments: Circumpolar, south in North America to Quebec, Colorado, Nevada, and California. Sparse.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits north facing banks, growing in a narrow zone in rock crevices and seeps just above the high water level. Assoc: Alnus spp., and pteridophytes and conifers. physicalDescription: A perennial herb from rhizomes, usually 1-2 m tall.  Leaves pinnately divided with 1-4 pairs of small (sometimes inconspicuous) leaflets and a large terminal leaflet, which is typically 8-20 cm wide and palmately lobed into 5-7 toothed sections. Flowers are numerous and occur in groups with the appearance of a flat top. Flower petals are white and about 6 mm long.  Fruit is a dry, brownish, hairy achene with a flattened body 4 mm long and a persistent style 2-3 mm long.
globalRangeComments: Endemic to northwestern Oregon and southwestern Washington, in coastal river systems (e.g. the Trask, Wilson, and Tillamook rivers, Oregon and the Naselle river, Washington) and high elevation Coast Range peaks. Most occurrences are found in Pacific County, Washington, Tillamook County, Oregon, and Lincoln County, Oregon.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: I. rhypara var. rhypara grows on outcrops of light-colored ash tuff and of poorly sorted volcanic ash deposited with riverbed gravels. Surrounding vegetation community type is Artemisia tridentata/Agropyron spicatum. The plants can sometimes be seen growing in neat rows caused by their rooting in the fissures of the underlying bedrock.

ecologyComments: Castilleja flava var. rustica’s relationship with grazing management actions, wildfire or prescribed fire are not well understood. Projecting the influence of a history of those impacts is equally difficult to do. That picture is also complicated by its probable connection to Artemisia tridentata and its relationship with these environmental stressors. Castilleja flava var. rustica patches are limited and often found along grassland ridgelines that are desirable locations for fire suppression actions – machine or hand lines. We have observed changes in the composition of and structure of many of the grassland habitats within which Castilleja flava var. rustica and Artemisia tridentata on the Wallowa-Whitman National Forest without yet understanding the consequences to this rare species. So although apparently numerous within its patches we don’t understand the limiting factors of those patches, the historical extent of those patches, or know the population trend. Thus it would seem that Castilleja flava var. rustica is vulnerable to impact by a suite of modern stressors. (specialist expertise – J. M. Hustafa, April 2024)

physicalDescription: This annual plant is inconspicuous where it grows among grasses. It grows 4 to 10 inches tall (10-40 cm), is usually branched and has gray-green hairy foliage with a purple tinge. Flowers are whitish in color, puckered-looking, and tipped with purplish red. There are many in spike and they are less than an inch long (15-25mm), about the same size as the calyx.

physicalDescription:
Diplacus clivicola is a small, generally single-stemmed annual with opposite, mostly elliptic leaves and large, pink, showy flowers. The entire plant is covered with glandular hairs that emit a musky odor when rubbed between the fingers (Lorain and Moseley 1989).

Recent work with the taxon (Lorain and Moseley 1989, Lorain and Moseley 1990, Lorain 1991,1992) has identified additional characteristics that are especially helpful for identification during field investigations. These investigators described Diplacus clivicola as having "distinctly pink" flowers and a musky, sweet smell when the herbage is rubbed.
globalRangeComments: Diplacus clivicola occurs in the western United States, in northern Idaho, Oregon, and Montana (FNA 2019). Although most of the floras of the Pacific Northwest (Hitchcock and Cronquist 1973) describe this taxon as occurring in Washington, only one documented record by George Vasey in 1889 exists for the state, and this occurrence has not been relocated. As of 1992 no extant locations are known from any portion of Washington (Lorain 1992). Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1994 and 2025 (RARECAT 2024, GBIF 2025, iNaturalist 2025, NatureServe 2025, SEINet 2025).

physicalDescription: A prostrate to sub-erect perennial herb, growing in masses. Plants are sparsely glandular-villous, with hairs that are slimy or sticky and transparent. Each plant has few to several stems which are slender, winged and sparsely branched with long internodes. There are 3-7 pairs of opposite leaves per stem; leaves are broadly lance-shaped to egg-shaped with triangular to heart-shaped bases; margins are shallowly toothed to smooth and leaf stalks (petioles) are as long or longer than the leaf blades. Along the flowering portion of the stem (inflorescence), pairs of flowers emerge from the leaf axils. Each flower has a narrow stalk (pedicel) that is slightly winged at the base and a green calyx with a narrow, triangular tube. Flowers are weakly two-lipped with cone-shaped corollas that are light yellow with red or purple spots on the throat and lower lobes. Fruits are oval, hairless capsules; seeds are egg-shaped, blunt, and wrinkled (Oregon Flora Project 2009).
globalRangeComments: Erythranthe hymenophylla occurs in the northwestern United States, only in northeastern Oregon, central Idaho, and western Montana. Most locations are in the Snake River drainage, within Hells Canyon. It is known from the deep canyons of the Horse and Cow Creek drainages in eastern Wallowa County, Oregon, and across the Snake River in western Idaho County, Idaho, within Hells Canyon (Flora of North America Editorial Committee 2019, GBIF 2023, Meinke 1995, MNHP 2023, NatureServe 2023, SEINet 2023).

globalRangeComments: Penstemon janishiae occurs in the western United States, where it is found largely in the Great Basin physiographic region (FNA 2019). Specifically, from very northeastern California in the Modoc Plateau region (Hickman 1993) and southern southeastern Oregon, to central and northeastern Nevada (Washoe, Elko, Humboldt, Nye, Lander, Eureka, and White Pine counties), and north to southwestern Idaho, in Owyhee County (FNA 2019). globalRangeComments: Whitebark Pine occurs in subalpine and timberline zones from west-central British Columbia east to west-central Alberta and south to central Idaho, southwestern Wyoming, and southern California (Murray, 2005; Ward et al., 2006). Its distribution is split into two broad sections, one following the Coast and Cascade ranges and the Sierra Nevada, and the other following the northern Rocky Mountains. Scattered populations occur between the two sections in Great Basin regions of eastern Washington and Oregon and northern Nevada (Fryer 2002, Burns and Honkala 1990). Although historical sources include Utah in the distribution, more recent workers have not found it to occur there (FNA 1993). The easternmost extent of the species is in the Wind River Range in Wyoming (USFWS 2016). COSEWIC (2010) evaluated current estimates of the extent of occurrence of Pinus albicaulis and found the best estimates to be 190,067 sq km in Canada and 147,000 sq km in the U.S. for a total of 337,067 sq. km. (COSEWIC 2010).

globalRangeComments: Limber pine is a species whose distribution has changed from continuous to patchy since the last glacial period. Approximately 14,000 years ago, Limber Pine was widespread along the eastern slope of the Colorado Front Range in the central Rocky Mountains (Schoettle 2004). Now it has a widespread but patchy distribution spanning a broad latitudinal and elevational range (1500-3600m) in the western United States and Canada. It occurs in the northern, central, and southern Rocky Mountains, and the Great Basin regions from British Columbia and Alberta in Canada, south through Oregon, Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, Nevada, Utah, Colorado to New Mexico. Isolated populations occur in the Dakotas, Nebraska, Arizona, eastern Oregon, and California (Burns and Honkala 1990, Johnson 2001). Cultivated populations can be found in New England, northern Europe, and New Zealand.

physicalDescription: Hair-like sedge is a densely tufted grass-like plant. Leaves are 0.75-4 mm wide and flat. Stems are very slender and are up to 60 cm long. The apex of the stem is terminated by a narrowly cylindrical cluster of male flowers 4-10 mm long. Towards the apex of the stem are 2-3 slender secondary branches that are terminated by cylindrical clusters of female flowers/fruits (spikes). The lower secondary branches and associated spikes droop. The female flowers mature into fruits (perigynia) which are 2.3-3.5 mm long and taper to a beak at their apex (Mackenzie 1931-1935, Ball 2002).
globalRangeComments: Carex capillaris has a circumboreal distribution, occurring in North America from Alaska, United States and throughout Canada south in the western United States to California east to New Mexico and South Dakota, and in the eastern United States to New York and Michigan west to Minnesota; it also occurs in Eurasia (FNA 2002). Range extent was estimated to be over 70 million square kilometers using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data documented between 1994 and 2025 (GBIF 2025, iNaturalist 2025, NatureServe 2025, RARECAT 2025, SEINet 2025). See individual entries for distribution details about the subspecific taxa.

physicalDescription: Bristly Sedge is a coarse, perennial, grasslike plant with clustered stems, 5-10 dm high, which arise from a short rhizome. The long, glabrous leaves are flat and 4-11 mm wide. Flowers are clustered in cylindical spikes, 2-7 cm long, which arise from the axils of the smaller upper leaves (bracts). The lowest bract leaf is much longer than the inflorescence. Male flowers are borne in a narrow spike at the top; 3-5 nodding female spikes, 15 mm thick, occur below. The glabrous, spreading, pale green, lance-shaped perigynia, 5-8 mm long, have a long beak ending in two long, slender, divergent lobes. The papery scales subtending the perigynia are 1-2 mm long with a pointed tip which can be up to 6 mm long. Each perigynia has 3 styles and a 3-sided achene.
globalRangeComments: Quebec to Minnesota and south; disjunct in the Pacific states; in Idaho, occurs in Bonner and Boundary Counties (Idaho Native Plant Society, 1992). In California, occurs in Contra Costa, Lake, Shasta, San Joaquin, and Sonoma Counties, extirpated in San Bernardino, Santa Cruz, and San Francisco Counties (Skinner, 1997). In Washington, known from Chelan, Jefferson, King, Pend Oreille, Skagit, Snohomish, Spokane, Thurston, and Whatcom Counties; historical in Kittitas and Walla Walla Counties (Washington Natural Heritage Program, 1997). South to Florida and Louisiana. Peripheral.

physicalDescription: Perennial tufted sedge with a short rhizome and obtuse-angled culms that are terete at the base. The leaves are gray-green and 1-2 mm in width, with brown-spotted sheaths. Heads are 3-4 cm long with 10 or more sessile spikes per head. The staminate flowers occur at the tip of the spike with the pistillate flowers at the base. The scales are light brown and acute; the perigynia are dark brown and broadly ovate and long-beaked.

physicalDescription: Northern bog sedge is a very fine grass-like perennial that grows in patches. Stems occur scattered along thread-like rhizomes and are 2-30 cm tall. Leaves are wispy and less than 1 mm wide. Stems have one flower/fruit cluster (spike) at their apex. These spikes vary from being composed of entirely male flowers, entirely female flowers, or having male flowers above and female flowers below. Fruits (perigynia) are 2.9-3.4 mm long (Cochrane 2002).
globalRangeComments: Carex gynocrates is chiefly boreal, occurring in eastern Asia, Greenland, and North America from Alaska, United States and throughout Canada south in the continental United States to Maine, New York, Pennsylvania (historical), Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, North Dakota, Colorado, Utah, Nevada, and Oregon (FNA 2002). It "is infrequent to rare southward, especially in the western cordillera" (FNA 2002). Range extent was estimated to be over 36 million square kilometers using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data documented between 1994 and 2025 (GBIF 2025, iNaturalist 2025, NatureServe 2025, RARECAT 2025, SEINet 2025).

physicalDescription: Idaho sedge is a rhizomatous perennial producing small clumps of stems that reach 20-35 cm in height.  The flat leaves are 2-4 mm in width and most are crowded near the base of the plant.  Flowers are borne in 1 to 4 oblong-cylindrical spikes, each 1-3 cm long, with the uppermost being larger than the others. The spikes form a narrow, interrupted head, subtended by small leaf-like bracts at the top of the stems.  Male flowers are absent or scattered among the female perigynia on the largest spike. Each perigynium is subtended by a narrowly oval, brown scale 2 to 3 times its length, with a tapered tip, membranous margins and a distinct pale center. The glabrous, egg-shaped perigynia are yellow-green and about 3 mm long, with a short beak. There are 3 stigmas and the seed is 3-sided.
globalRangeComments: Occurs in southwestern Montana, Idaho, California, Oregon, and Utah (FNA 2002 and Baldwin et al. 2012).

physicalDescription: Sharp-pointed Flatsedge is a grass-like, 5-20 cm high annual that forms tufts of stems. The few leaves occur near the base of the plant and are 1-2 mm wide. The inflorescence is subtended by 3-4 long, leaf-like bracts. Each flower consists only of a small, pointed, 2 mm long scale, which subtends a single stamen and ovary. Flowers are crowded opposite each other into flattened spikelets that are 3-7 mm long. The spikelets occur in globose clusters and are borne on very short to long stalks. The seed is triangular in cross-section.

physicalDescription:
Simple Kobresia is a sedge-like plant that forms small bunches with triangular stems up to 15 cm tall. The leaves, which are confined to near the base of the plant, are flat or rolled and ca. 1 mm wide. Dried sheaths and blades persist at the base of the plant. The 3-12 small spikes are borne in a loosely congested inflorescence at the top of the stem. Each spike is 5-15 mm long, is subtended by a small, brown, papery bract, and consists of a few flowers; male flowers with anthers are located above female flowers. Each female flower is composed of a small bract and a scale that is loosely wrapped around the ovary.

From CNHP Wetland Guide 2012: Growth Habit: strongly rhizomatous. Culms: 5-35 cm.
Leaves: basal sheaths dull, base of blade usually persistent. Blades: 2-20 cm x 0.2-1.5 mm
Inflorescence: usually compound, 10-35 x 3-8 mm.
Bracts: brown, margins hyaline, ovate to oblong-ovate.
Spikelets: proximal spikelet 1 flowered and pistillate or 2 flowered and androgynous; terminal and distal spikelets 1-flowered, staminate.
Pistillate Scales: brown, ovate, 2-3 mm, margins hyaline, midvein distinct almost to tip, apex obtuse to sub-acute.
Perigynia: brown, 2.5-3.2 mm, margins free to base, smooth.
globalRangeComments: Circumpolar, in North America from Alaska to Greenland south to New Brunswick, N Ontario, Alberta, and in the Rocky Mountains south to Montana, Utah, NW Wyoming, and C Colorado.

physicalDescription: Slender Bulrush is a tall, glabrous, grass-like perennial with firm, tubular stems that are 1-2 m tall and arising from stout brown rhizomes. The few leaves are borne near the base and have a sheath surrounding the stem, but the blade is small and tapers to a point. Numerous slender-stalked, solitary spikelets are borne on the spreading branch tips of an open, terminal inflorescence. Each egg-shaped spikelet is up to 17 mm long and has several flowers arranged in a tight spiral. Flowers consist of a single scale that is up to 5 mm long; it subtends 3 stamens and an ovary with 4 white bristles that are as long as the scales and arising from the base. The 3-sided achene is ca. 3 mm long with a short beak and 3 stigmas.
globalRangeComments: Schoenoplectus heterochaetus occurs in North America from Quebec west to Alberta (possibly extirpated) in Canada and in the United States from Vermont and Massachusetts (possibly extirpated) west to Oregon, Washington (possibly extirpated), and California, and centrally from Texas and Missouri north. Range extent was estimated to be over almost 4.4 million square kilometers using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data documented between 1993 and 2024 (GBIF 2024, iNaturalist 2024, NatureServe 2024, SEINet 2024).

physicalDescription: Pendulous bulrush is a glabrous, grass-like perennial with tufted stems, up to 15 dm (5 ft) tall. The several stem leaves are 3-10 mm wide. Numerous slender-stalked spikelets are borne in open groups in a branched, terminal inflorescence, usually 1 spikelet in each group sessile, the others long-stalked. The inflorescence is subtended by a leaf-like bract. Each cylindrical spikelet, 6-10 mm long, has numerous flowers arranged in a tight spiral. Flowers consist of a light brown, egg-shaped scale, ca. 2 mm long, with a green midvein, subtending 3 stamens and an ovary with 6 brown, twisted bristles, longer than the scales, arising from the base. The 3-sided seed (achene) is ca. 1 mm long with a short beak.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

physicalDescription: Water Bulrush is a rhizomatous perennial with slender, weak stems that are 20-80 cm long and which float on the water's surface rather than emerging from it. Leaves are long and flaccid and arise mainly from near the base of the plant. The inflorescence consists of a solitary spike subtended by a green, leaf-like bract that is 1-6 cm long and held nearly erect, appearing to be a continuation of the stem. The light brown spike is composed of numerous, membranous scales, each subtending a flower consisting of 3 stamens and an ovary with 6 slender bristles arising from the base. The ovary matures into a three-sided achene that is 2-4 mm long.
globalRangeComments: Spotty distribution from southern Alaska to Oregon, disjunct to Northeastern North America south to Georgia.

habitatDescription: Meadows and small openings, which fill with snow and/or water in winter and spring, and are variously dominated by grasses and sedges. Successional invasion of these meadows by Pinus contorta, Populus trichocarpa, Picea engelmannii and Spiraea douglasii occurs.
physicalDescription: A perennial herb up to 32 cm tall, although most plants are only 15-20 cm tall. The leaves are narrow and are typically, but not always, shorter than the stem. Both the stems and leaves are a pale green or blue-green in color. Each stem has 2-7 flowers on slender stalks (pedicels). Flowers are pale blue with a yellow spot in the center. The petal-like structures comprising the flower (tepals) are about 1.25 cm in length and pale blue in color. The anthers are yellow (adapted from WA NHP 1999).
ecologyComments: The meadows and small openings on which S. sarmentosum depend are probably mostly maintained by moisture and soil conditions, and fire could be a factor in maintaining or creating new habitat.

physicalDescription: Flowering Quillwort is a tufted annual with leafless stems that are 3-20 cm high. The linear basal leaves are 2-25 cm long, are round in cross-section, and have a broad base that sheaths each flower stem. Male, female, or bisexual flowers are borne in an open spike that is 5-40 mm long and at the tops of stems, which are shorter than the leaves. Additional female flowers may be found partly enclosed by the leaf sheaths. Male and bisexual flowers consist of a green elliptic bract that is 2-3 mm long and of a single stamen and/or a single ovary. Female flowers consist of a solitary ovary. The narrowly lance-shaped fruits of the spike are 3-5 mm long, flattened, and wing-margined. Fruits borne in the leaf sheaths are cylindrical, 3-angled, and have 3 small horns at the tip.
globalRangeComments: This species occurs in Western North America, Central America, and South America. It is introduced in Australia. Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1983 and 2023 (GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023, NatureServe 2023, SEINet 2023).

physicalDescription: Three-flowered Rush is a small, tufted, grass-like perennial with stems that are 5-15 cm high. The basal leaves are 2-10 cm long, round in cross-section, and divided internally into sections (septate). Stem leaves are lacking. 2-4 flowers are borne in a solitary, terminal cluster that is subtended by 2 brown, papery bracts which are as long as the head. Each flower is subtended by a single scale-like bract and has 6 pale brown perianth segments, or tepals, that are ca. 4 mm long with rounded tips. There are 6 stamens. The brown capsule is 3-5 mm high and is rounded on top with a short beak; it is about as long as the tepals. Each seed is 1-2 mm long with a narrow, papery wing on each end.
globalRangeComments: Alaska to Newfoundland, south to British Columbia, Montana, Utah, and Colorado.

physicalDescription: Columbia Water-meal, a minute floating aquatic perennial, is among the world's smallest flowering plants. The plant body is rootless and thalloid, with no distinction between stem and leaf. The symmetrical, globular, uniformly green thalli are less than 1.5 mm long, smooth and rounded on the back, and floating just below the surface of the water. The plants rarely flower and for the most part reproduce vegetatively by budding. They often grow in large colonies.
ecologyComments: It overwinters in the form of turions, on the bottom of the water.

habitatDescription: Inhabits chaparral, open Oregon white oak woodlands and savannas around dry thickets and on rocky slopes, with heavy clay soils. Assoc. species: Amelanchier pallida, Quercus garryana, Q. vaccinifolia, Q. breweri, Phlox diffusa, Arctostaphylos nevadensis, Thlaspi montanum, Spirea densiflora, Festuca idahoensis, Stipa lemmonii, and Microseris laciniata ssp. detlingii. || Openings in and edges of oak woodlands.
ecologyComments: Occurs in heavy clay soils, in grassey openings. The habitat formerly was grassland - chapparal - oak savanna matrix kept open by wildfire. The combination of grazing and fire supression followed by severe fires has altered the habitat, creating a mosaic of dense white oak thickets and annual grasslands. Restoring the native ecosystems will be quite difficult in these areas.

habitatDescription: Howell’s mariposa lily is an Oregon endemic that occurs on dry, rocky slopes with soils that are wet in the spring but dry quickly thereafter (Mullens et al. 2017; ODA n.d.). It is restricted to serpentinite soils of ultramafic derivation, high metal concentrations and low Calcium to Magnesium ratios (Fredricks 1992). It has been recorded on Eightlar, Dubakella, and Pearsol soil series and the soils have an average pH of 7.2, are clay loams or clays that are stony, montane, and with dark reddish-brown subsoils (Fredricks 1992). It occurs in the Illinois River valley in areas with sparse vegetation (ODA n.d.). It occurs at elevations of 300 to 800 m in Ceanothus dominated slopes and open stands of Pinus jeffreyi (Mullens et al. 2017). Occurs in open, Pinus jeffreyi savanna, always on serpentine soils at lower or middle elevations, often in brushy areas. Occurs on slopes and flats, usually with eastern or southeastern exposure. Associated with Ceanothus cuneatus, Arctostaphylos viscida shrublands and Pinus jeffreyi. Associated dominants are Festuca idahoensis, Stipa lemmonii, Danthonia californica, Ceanothus pumilis, Microseris howellii, and Senecio hesperius. Chamaecyparis lawsoniana, Notholithocarpus densiflorus, Pinus jeffreyi, P. lambertiana, P. monticola, P. ponderosa, Pseudotsuga menziesii and Quercus garryana (Fredricks 1992; ODA n.d.; ORBIC 2022). Associated shrubs include Arctostaphylos canescens, A. viscida, Ceanothus cuneatus, C. pumilus, Garrya buxifolia, Holodiscus discolor, Q. vacciniifolia, Rhododendron occidentalis, and Umbellularia californica (Fredricks 1992; ODA n.d.; ORBIC 2022). Associated herbs include Allium amplectens, A. alcifolium, Antennaria howellii, Arabis aculeolata, A. cernua, Arnica nevadensis, Balsamorhiza hookeri, B. sericea, Calochortus tolmiei, Cardamine nuttallii, Erigeron cervinus, Eriogonum umbellatum, Eriophyllum lanatum, Erythronium citrinum, Eucephalus tomentellus, Galium, Hastingsia alba, Horkelia sericata, Iris, Lomatium triternatum, Microseris douglasii, M. howellii, Monardella odoratissima, M. purpurea, Packera cana, Phlox speciosa, Ranunculus uncinatus, Sabulina howellii, Sedum laxum, Senecio, Toxicoscordion micranthum, Trillium rivale, Triteleia hyacinthina, Viola lobata, and V. cuneata (Fredricks 1992; ODA n.d.; ORBIC 2022). Associated graminoids include Bromus sitchensis var. carinatus, Carex serpenticola, Danthonia californica, Elymus glaucus, Eriocoma lemmonii, Elymus multisetus, Festuca californica, Festuca idahoensis, Melica geyeri, and Poa secunda and associated fern species include Aspidotis densa (Fredricks 1992; ODA n.d.; ORBIC 2022)
physicalDescription: This lily-like plant has an erect, slender bloom stalk that grows up to 18 inches tall (4.5 dm) with 1 or 2 wide upright, bell-shaped, pure white flowers (or white with a greenish tinge) with brownish bases which are less than an inch long (2.5 cm). Dense white to brownish to greenish hairs cover the dark base of the petals. Sepals are white and narrow. The capsule is elliptic, erect, less than 3/4 of an inch long. A single basal leaf sometimes longer that the flower stalk and about 1/3 inch wide (10mm) is densely hairy on the upper surface in the middle.
ecologyComments: Relationships to fire which has been artificially restricted from its habitat need to be explored. The effects of fire on Howell’s mariposa-lily are not well understood (Fredricks 1992; USDA 2022b). Fire could provide the open habitat needed for this species but could also promote the germination of shrubs that may out compete it (Fredricks 1992). Plants with bulbs are generally thought to survive low-intensity fires.
globalRangeComments: Known only from southwestern Oregon, Douglas and Josephine Counties, Oregon.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits moist, rocky serpentine slopes and flats. Associated species: Pinus jeffreyi, Ceanothus cuneatus, Arctostaphylos viscida, Rhododendron occidentale, and various grasses.
physicalDescription: This lily-like plant has one or two stout 3-5 inch tall (8-12 cm) bloom stalks with 2 to 3 bright lavender upright flowers on each.  Short purple hairs are found near the base of the petals. Sepals have no distinct color.   Capsules nod, are ovoid and less than 3/4 inch long.  The basal leaf is as long as the bloom stalk and 1/3 inch wide (8-10mm).  There is a stem leaf just below the blooms that is 3 to 4 inch long by 1/10 inch wide (3mm).
globalRangeComments: Only known from type locality (Sexton Mountain, Oregon), where last seen in 1948.

ecologyComments: Most C. longebarbatus var. peckii habitats are in high fire frequency areas, and the plant may be somewhat dependent on natural disturbance.

habitatDescription: All populations are on serpentine soils, most often on shady, N-facing, mesic sites near ridgelines. Typically grows in serpentine grasslands and forest margins. Associated species include: Calocedrus decurrens, Festuca idahoensis, Pinus jeffreyi, Calochortus tolmiei, Allium bolanderi ssp. mirabile, Pinus ponderosa, Rhododendron occidentalis, Pseudotsuga menziesii, Silene hookeri, and Arbutus menziesii. || Restricted to serpentine soils, grasslands, openings in and edges of mixed woodlands, often comprised of Jeffrey pine, Douglas fir, Incense cedar, or madrone.
ecologyComments: Germination appears to be enhanced following soil disturbance (such as occurs following fire). Overgrazing by sheep has reduced some populations, but the effect of moderate grazing or adjacent logging is unclear.

physicalDescription: This lily-like plant has white to pink flowers (1 to 4) gracefully nodding on a stem 16-30 cm long. Petals strongly arch back in sunlight, are nearly 5 cm long and have a narrow yellow band at the base. A pair of plain green to slightly mottled leaves up to 10 cm long and with very short stalks are found at the base of flowering plants.
ecologyComments: Occurs in partially shaded, coastal but montane bog margins, or very moist meadow habitats.

habitatDescription: Openings in predominantly oak woodlands but also reported from mixed conifer-deciduous forests and conifer stands. Associated species: Brodiaea spp., Ceanothus cuneatus, Phacelia spp., Microseris spp., and Erythronium spp. Openings in oak woodlands, mixed conifer-deciduous or conifer forests
physicalDescription: This lily-like plant has 1/2 inch long (4 cm) deep red to maroon flared bell-shaped flowers with yellow mottling on flowering stems that grow up to 28 inches tall (70 cm). Stamens are shorter than petals. Stems and leaves are waxy bluish green to purple mottled. Leaves usually grow in two whorls of three with additional scattered pairs along the stem; the largest nearest the base are up to 6 inches long (15 cm) by 1/2 inch wide (1.5 cm). Nonflowering individuals are recognizable only by their single basal leaves. The dry capsule is roundish with broad thin papery edges.
ecologyComments: Fire supression in these habitats has resulted in open oak, fir, and madrone woodlands becoming more closed canopy forests, reducing the habitat for this species. Shrubs such as Ceanothus cuneatus and Arctostaphylos sp. have become large and decadent, which also reduces habitat potential for this plant. Some reintroduction of fire is critical for this species' long term survival.
globalRangeComments: Fritillaria gentneri occurs at scattered localities in southwest Oregon (U.S.A.) along the Rogue and Illinois River drainages in Josephine and Jackson Counties. It is also known from two sites, about one mile apart, in far northern California.

habitatDescription: Occurs in two, moist serpentine habitats. Darlingtonia californica, Helenium biglovei, Rhododendron occidentalis, and Chamaecyparis lawsoniana are associated with both of these communities. The largest populations are in serpentine Darlingtonia bogs. These are either hillslope bogs or hanging bogs located above the larger rivers and streams. Associated species include other endemics such as Gentiana setigera, Viola occidentalis and Castilleja miniata ssp. elata, as well as Narthesium californica and Sanguisorba microcephala. It also is found in low elevation serpentine riparian habitats, both on small streams, and along the larger creeks and rivers. These are shrubbier habitats with more Rhododendron occidentalis and Chamaecyparis. Other associated species include Cyprepidium californicum, Carex mendocinensis and Umbellaria californica.
ecologyComments: Usually occurs near running water, both along streams and within Darlingtonia bogs. Always occurs on extremely serpentine areas at low elevations.
globalRangeComments: Hastingsia bracteosa var. atropurpurea is known only from the Illinois River Valley, Josephine County, southwestern Oregon, USA; most occurrences are between Tennessee Mountain and O'Brien (Oregon Department of Agriculture 2008). Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1993 and 2024 (CPNWH 2024, iNaturalist 2024, NatureServe 2024, SEINet 2024). The range extent would expand to 130 km² if plants were relocated at one historical occurrence east of O'Brien (NatureServe 2024).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1999. A synonymized checklist and atlas with biological attributes for the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. First edition. In: Kartesz, J.T., and C.A. Meacham. Synthesis of the North American Flora, Version 1.0. North Carolina Botanical Garden, Chapel Hill, N.C.

habitatDescription: Occurs in two, moist serpentine habitats. Associated species include other endemics such as Gentiana setigera, Viola occidentalis and Castilleja miniata ssp. elata, as well as Narthesium californica and Sanguisorba microcephala. Hastingsia bracteosa also occurs in riparian habitats, both on small streams, and along the larger creeks and rivers. These are shrubbier habitats with more Rhododendron occidentalis and Chamaecyparis. Other associated species include Cyprepidium californicum, Carex mendocinensis and Umbellaria californica.

ecologyComments: Usually occurs near running water, both along streams and within Darlingtonia fens. Always occurs on extremely serpentine areas at low elevations.

habitatDescription: Undisturbed mixed conifer/hardwood forest with filtered sunlight. Douglas fir is almost always present. In southwestern Oregon, madrone and Pacific dogwood can be indicators. In northeastern Oregon, Ponderosa pine can be important. Parent material and moisture requirements vary widely. Shade varies from 60 to 100 %. In Washington, populations found mostly in association with Abies grandis. Harris hypothesizes that a fungus associated with deer or elk feces is required for seed germination, given frequency with which populations are found near game trails.
physicalDescription: Clustered Lady's-slipper is a perennial with densely hairy, solitary stems, which are 5-20 cm tall and arise from a rhizome. There is a single leaf wrapped around the base of the stem and one pair of sessile, opposite leaves located near the top of the stem; these leaves are broadly elliptic to oval-shaped and are 4-8 cm broad. The 2-4 flowers are tightly clustered at the top of the stem, and each is subtended by a green, lance-shaped bract. The 3 narrowly lance-shaped sepals are 12-25 mm long and greenish brown to purplish with purple lines or spots; the lower 2 are united nearly to the tip. The 2 upper petals are similar to the sepals in shape and color; the lower petal is pouch-shaped, shorter than the sepals, and greenish yellow with brownish-purple margins and often a purple tinge. The ovary and mature capsule are densely hairy.
ecologyComments: Population numbers are often small, 1-20 plants, although there are occasional populations with 500+ plants in a few acres, usually in old-growth Douglas fir habitats along stream terraces. Fire scars are always present in the larger populations.
globalRangeComments: Cypripedium fasciculatum occurs in disjunct areas of mountain ranges in the west (Coast Ranges, Cascades, Sierra Nevadas, Rockies), from Washington, Idaho to Montana, Oregon to central California, and Utah, Wyoming, and Colorado (Flora of North America Editorial Committee 2002). Falsely reported from British Columbia (Kartesz 1999).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

physicalDescription: Minute muhly is a tufted annual grass with stems up to 3 dm (1 ft) tall. The inrolled leaf blades are 1-2 mm wide, and the membranous ridge onthe blade where it meets the stem (ligule) is 1-3 mm high with jagged margins. Plants are sparsely hairy below stem nodes and on upper leaf surfaces. The single-flowered spikelets, ca. 1 mm long, are borne on the ends of long ascending stalks in an open, terminal inflorescence that is often half the plant's total height. The glumes are sparsely hairy along the margins and sometimes on the back, and both the glumes and lemmas lack awns.
globalRangeComments: Muhlenbergia minutissima occurs in western North America from Washington east to South Dakota, south to Texas, and west to California in the United States, and into southern Mexico (FNA 2003). habitatDescription: Grows in scablands with Poa secunda (Sandberg's bluegrass) associations, characterized by shallow and stony soils subject to heat and drought in summer and frost action in the winter. Has been noted in the following community types in NE Oregon: Poa secunda-Danthonia unispicata, Artemisia tridentata/Poa secunda, Eriogonum strictum-Poa secunda, and Eriogonum douglasii-Poa secunda. Central OR community types include: Artemisia rigida/Poa secunda and Lomatium cous-Poa secunda. All aspects; slopes reported from 0% to 20%. Major associated species include: Poa secunda, Eriogonum spp., Lomatium spp., Allium spp., Lewisia rediviva, Sedum stenopetalum, Blepharipappus scaber, Penstemon deustus, Bromus brizaeformis. Other rare plant species associates: Collomia macrocalyx, Allium tolmiei var. platyphyllum.
ecologyComments: Lithosolic sites.
globalRangeComments: Known from Kittitas and Yakima counties in central WA and from Wasco, Crook, and Wallowa counties in OR.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Achnatherum speciosum occurs in semi-arid and arid regions of the southwestern United States, northern Mexico, and in Chile south to central Argentina (FNA 2007).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits moist meadows and marshland at ca 750 to 1200 m in association with aquatic and semiaquatic species.
globalRangeComments: Lophochlaena oregona is known from disjunct locations in Lake, Klamath, and Union Counties, Oregon, USA. Each disjunct population occupies about 10 km. No intermediate populations were located in spite of a fairly extensive search during the 1986 field season. Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1993 and 2024 (iNaturalist 2024, OSU 2024, NatureServe 2024).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

ecologyComments: in association with Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda), stiff sagebrush (Artemisia rigida), one-spike danthonia (Danthonia unispicata) and biscuitroot (Lomatium spp.).
globalRangeComments: Limited to two disjunct areas in the state, the northeastern corner of Oregon in the Wallowa Mountains (area of 30 mile x 15 mile) and the Ochoco Mountains in central Oregon (area of 3.5 mile x 1 mile) although total apparently suitable habitat is more extensive.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1999. A synonymized checklist and atlas with biological attributes for the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. First edition. In: Kartesz, J.T., and C.A. Meacham. Synthesis of the North American Flora, Version 1.0. North Carolina Botanical Garden, Chapel Hill, N.C.

globalRangeComments: Potamogeton diversifolius occurs in wetlands in the United States, southwestern Canada, and Mexico. In the United States it primarily occurs from Massachusetts to Minnesota south to Kansas, Texas, and Florida, with outlying and scattered populations in South Dakota, Wyoming, Colorado, Montana, Idaho, Arizona, and California, and in southern Alberta and southern British Columbia, Canada. It has been documented in about one third of the states in Mexico. The range extent is about 8.5 million square kilometers (GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023, NatureServe 2023, Villaseñor 2016).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Potamogeton foliosus ssp. fibrillosus occurs in the northwestern United States, from Washington south to California, and east to Idaho, Utah, and Wyoming (FNA 2000). It is considered historical in Oregon (Oregon Biodiversity Information Center 1988). Range extent was estimated at 242,984 sq km using NatureServe Network occurrence data, CalFlora observations, data from the Utah Rare Plants Database, and herbarium specimens collected between 1984 and 2025, and estimated at 666,177 sq km when historical collections are included (Utah Natural Heritage Program 2021, CalFlora 2025, CCH2 2025, CPNWH 2025, GBIF 2025, NatureServe 2025, RARECAT 2025, SEINet 2025).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1999. A synonymized checklist and atlas with biological attributes for the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. First edition. In: Kartesz, J.T., and C.A. Meacham. Synthesis of the North American Flora, Version 1.0. North Carolina Botanical Garden, Chapel Hill, N.C.

habitatDescription: Thickets and streambanks, below 5000 ft.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Jordan's Maidenhair Fern occurs in the western United States, and Baja California in northwestern Mexico. It occurs in the Coast Range and Sierra Nevada from southwestern Oregon to the mountains of southern California and northern Baja California. The range extent was estimated to be about 300,000 square kilometers, using herbarium specimens and photo-based observations documented between 1992 and 2023 (CCH2 Portal 2023, Flora of North America Editorial Committee 1993, GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Moist seeps in basalt cliff crevices
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Rock crevices
globalRangeComments: Myriopteris intertexta is endemic to the western United States from south-central Washington south to California, west to northwestern Arizona and Utah (FNA 1993, Legler and Giblin 2024, SEINet 2026). Range extent was estimated to be approximately 750,000 square kilometers using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data documented between 1994 and 2026 (RARECAT 2025, GBIF 2026, iNaturalist 2026, NatureServe 2026, SEINet 2026).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Grows on limestone or other calcareous substrates, usually in crevices on vertical rock faces, often sheltered under some sort of rock overhand. Mostly on N- and E-facing slopes.
physicalDescription: This delicate, slender perennial fern has two kinds of fronds, sterile and fertile, and grows only 1-2 together unlike Cryptogramma crispa, which has robust fronds that are crowded together on a short rhizome.
ecologyComments: Grows in limestone or other calcareous substrates and rock crevices which contain moisture seepage.
globalRangeComments: Nearly circumpolar. Northern North America. Alaska to Labrador south to Oregon, Montana, Iowa, Michigan, and West Virginia, with disjunct populations in Wyoming, New Mexico, and Utah. Europe, Asia. (Welsh 1974; Porsild and Cody 1980; USDA NRCS 2012).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Coffee Fern (Pellaea andromedifolia) occurs in western North America, in Baja California and Baja California Sur, Mexico and California and southwestern Oregon in the United States. Range extent was estimated to be 490,000 square kilometers using herbarium specimens and photo-based observations documented between 1992 and 2023 (CCH2 Portal 2023, Flora of North America Editorial Committee 1993, GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023, Villaseñor 2016).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Rock crevices of talus slopes and boulder fields at mid-to high-elevations.
globalRangeComments: Bridges' Cliffbrake (Pellaea bridgesii) occurs in the western United States, in the Sierra Nevada of California, and western Nevada, with disjunct occurrences in northeastern Oregon and Idaho. The range extent was estimated to be 320,000 square kilometers, using herbarium specimens and photo-based observations documented between 1992 and 2023 (CCH2 Portal 2023, Flora of North America Editorial Committee 1993, GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Rock outcrops and ridges, with partial canopy cover and at least partial shade
globalRangeComments: Southwestern South Dakota to Arizona and Texas and along the California Sierra Nevada to southwestern Oregon, with a disjunct population in West Virginia. Based on specimen records, this species appears to be common in Europe.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Crevices of rocky cliffs of limestone substrate at high elevation
physicalDescription: Rhizomes short and scaly, but lacking median nerve; fronds 1 cm wide, up to 10 cm tall, densely tufted; stipes with deep groove and broad green margins, brown in lower part only, glabrous; pinnae herbaceous; sori near indistinct midvein (Hulten 1968).
globalRangeComments: This species is scattered across the temperate region of the Northern Hemisphere in North America, Europe and Asia. It is documented in Yukon, southwestern District of Mackenzie, British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario, Quebec, and Nova Scotia in Canada; central Alaska, Vermont, north New York, northern Missouri, Wisconsin (Dear County), Montana, South Dakota, Utah, northeast Nevada, Oregon, Washington, northern California in the United States, and Mexico. It is also found in southeast Greenland, Iceland and Eurasia. In California, it is only known from the Sierra Buttes (Skinner 1997). In Idaho, it occurs in Bear Lake and Clearwater Counties (Idaho Native Plant Society 1992). In Nevada, it is known only from Elko County (Kartesz 1988).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Among rocks in mesophytic, shaded conditions, from low to mid-elevation mixed forests to deep cracks in lava flows
globalRangeComments: Dryopteris filix-mas is found across the northern hemisphere. In North America, it occurs in largely disjunct populations in southern Greenland, western North America from British Columbia to Saskatchewan south to California and Texas, and northeastern North America from Ontario to Newfoundland south to Illinois and Maine (Cody and Britton 1985, Kartesz 1999). It is also found across northern and southern Europe, North Africa, Central Asia, and Siberia (POWO 2024).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: Polystichum californicum occurs in western North America from southwestern British Columbia, Canada south in the United States to California where it is restricted to the Coast Ranges and Sierra-Cascade axis and most abundant in the North Coast Range north of San Francisco (FNA 2002). Range extent was estimated to be over 260,000 square kilometers using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data documented between 1994 and 2025 (GBIF 2025, iNaturalist 2025, NatureServe 2025, SEINet 2025).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

physicalDescription: This fern has evergreen fronds that are 9-35 cm long and clustered on a short, ascending rhizome. Each frond consists of a scale-covered petiole, or stipe, that is 2-11 cm long and a narrowly lance-shaped blade, or lamina, that is 7-23 cm long and deeply lobed into 20-40 leaflets, or pinnae. Each pinna has a toothed and spiny margin, and the lower ones are lobed at the base. Spores are borne in small clusters, or sori, that are partially covered by a membranous disk, or indusium, that is located on the undersides of the upper pinnae.
globalRangeComments: The species ranges from C. BC to N. CA, east to ID and UT. Its known distribution in Canada is very limited (Cody, 1989). It is also found in MT, OR, and WA (TNC Element files).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Found in damp areas, usually near streams
physicalDescription: Stiff club-moss, a perennial, has elongated horizontal stems trailing on the ground, rooting at intervals, mostly unbranched. Upright shoots are clustered, mainly unbranched or sparsely branched near the base, 1.2-1.6 cm in diameter and to 20 cm or more in height; annual bud constrictions abrupt and conspicuous. Lateral branchlets few but without the annual constrictions. Leaves dark green, spreading to reflexed, linear-lanceolate (lance-shaped) 2.5 x 6 mm, stiff, sharp pointed, lacking a hair tip. Strobili (cone-like structure composed of overlapping scales bearing spore-containing structures) sessile at the ends of the shoots, solitary, 15-30 x 3.5-4.5 mm. Sporophylls (scales of the strobili) to 3.4 x 2 mm, abruptly narrowed to pointed tips.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Coniferous forests of Pseudotsuga menziesii, Tsuga mertensiana, Pico contorta, sometimes open areas near ridgetops and meadows. Also may grow with Lycopodium sitchensis and L. clavatum
globalRangeComments: Greenland and Quebec; west to Alaska; south to Maine, northern New York, northern Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Alberta, northern Idaho, and Washington.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Wet areas, in bogs, deflation plain, streambanks, meadows. Soils of peat, sand, occasional clay, usually highly acidic.
physicalDescription: Northern Bog Clubmoss resembles a large moss. It has prostrate or arching stems that root at irregular intervals and give rise to erect branches that are up to 10 cm high. The narrow, pointed leaves are 4-8 mm long and clothe the stems and branches in 8-10 ranks. Each spore is subtended by a bract, or sporophyll, that is similar to the leaves and borne in dense spikes at the top of erect branches. It is difficult to distinguish the fertile and sterile portions of the branches.
ecologyComments: Usually highly acidic soils
globalRangeComments: Europe, northeastern North America, and spotty distribution in northwestern North America.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

globalRangeComments: American Pillwort (Pilularia americana) is known from North America (United States and Mexico) and South America (Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Venezuela, and Peru). In North America it occurs in Washington, Oregon, and most commonly in California, south into Baja California, Mexico. It also occurs in the Southern Great Plains from Kansas south to the Llano Uplift in Texas, Interior Highlands of Arkansas and Missouri, Interior Low Plateau of Tennessee and Alabama, and in the Appalachian and Piedmont regions of Georgia, Tennessee, South Carolina, and West Virginia. The range extent was estimated to be 16 million square kilometers using herbarium specimens and photo-based observations documented between 1992 and 2023 (CCH2 Portal 2023, Flora of North America Editorial Committee 1993, GBIF 2023, iNaturalist 2023, León et al. 2018).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Open woods; swamp area in young to mid-aged densely forested cedar-hemlock; small grassy opening among lodgepole; near springs with cedar overstory. Can grow with B. lunaria, B. multifidum, B. pendunculosum, B. pinnatum, B. minganense and B. simplex
globalRangeComments: Var. lanceolatum extends from Alaska to Oregon, Arizona, and New Mexico.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Moist, wet areas; grassy openings in coniferous forests. Associated species include: Botrychium virginianum, B. ascendens, B. crenulatum, B. minganense, B. multifidum, B. pedunculosum, B. lanceolatum, B. pinnatum, B. simplex.
physicalDescription: Moonwort is a very small, perennial fern with a single aboveground frond. The dark-green frond is usually about 4 inches long and can be seen through mid-summer. It is divided into two leaves above a common stalk. The sterile leaf is usually dark green, thick, and fleshy. It has up to 9 usually overlapping pairs of broadly fan-shaped leaflets (pinnae). The top edges are rounded and smooth or wavy or rarely have teeth. The fertile leaf is longer than the sterile leaf with branches that bear grape-like sporangia. Spores germinate underground and develop into tiny, non-photosynthetic gametophytes which depend on an fungus for nourishment.
globalRangeComments: Botrychium lunaria appears in North and South America, Eurasia, Australia, and New Zealand. In North America it occurs from Newfoundland and Labrador west to Alaska, and south to Massachusetts, New York, Michigan, Minnesota, Saskatchewan, New Mexico, Arizona, and California.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Inhabits fine pumice gravel without humus at elevations above 2400 m. In winter the sites are covered with up to 10 feet of snow which leaves the soil extremely dry during July and August. Assoc. species: Carex breweri and Eriogonum species. Also known from frost pockets in Lodgepole pine forests with bitterbrush, in areas with deep, sterile pumice. || Pumice-derived soils in lodgepole pine-bitterbrush communities. Also on open ridgetops in raw pumice.
physicalDescription: A small deciduous grape-fern, growing 3 to 8 1/2 inches tall (8-22 cm) with both sterile and fertile fronds. Sterile fronds grow upright,are leathery, stemless, small up to about 1 1/2 inches long (3.8 cm) and are divided into thirds then cut again, segments are roundish. Fertile fronds are larger than the sterile fronds, cut into a comb-like divisions and have spore baring structures that are round and yellow colored.
ecologyComments: Grows only on pumice
globalRangeComments: Botrychium pumicola occurs in the Pacific Northwest of the United States in central and southern Oregon and northern California. It is found in Paulina Mountains and the Crater Lake area of Oregon (Deschutes, Klamath, and Lake Counties) and in the vicinity of Mt. Shasta in California (Siskiyou County) (CNDDB 2023).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

otherStates: MT, UT, WA, AB, BC, SK
habitatDescription: All sites between 5,000 and 5,500 ft. elevation with nearly full sun, gentle slopes and open meadow plant associations in mesic soil.
physicalDescription: Peculiar moonwort is a small perennial fern with a single above ground frond. The frond varies in height up to about 15 cm tall, is glaucous green, somewhat succulent, and divided into two similar segments which share a common stalk. The segments may be unbranched in small plants or branched in larger plants and are both fertile and bear grape-like sporangia. Spores germinate underground and develop into minute, subterranean, non-photosynthetic gametophytes which depend on an endophytic fungus for nourishment.
globalRangeComments: Botrychium paradoxum occurs in the western United States from south central Utah and Colorado northward to Montana and Washington and into southern British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan with a disjunct occurrence in the Sierra Mountains of east-central California (Farrar 2011). There is one possible but unverified observation in Alaska which is not included in the area calculations (iNaturalist 2025). Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimens, photo-based observations, and NatureServe Network occurrence data collected between 1994 and 2025 (GBIF 2025, iNaturalist 2025, NatureServe 2025, RARECAT 2025, SEINet 2025, CPNWH 2025).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

county: Bake, Croo, Gran, Hood, Linn, Mari, Unio, Wall, Wasc, Whee
habitatDescription: Thuja plicata forests; also been found along grassy trail edges. Associated species include: B. lunaria, B. lanceolatum, B. boreale, B. minganense.
physicalDescription: Mountain Moonwort is a small perennial fern with a single aboveground frond. The frond varies in height but may reach a height of 12 cm. It is a dull, glaucous gray-green, somewhat succulent, and divided into two segments which share a relatively short common stalk. The sterile segment is once pinnatifid with well separated, irregular, angular, ascending lobes with entire or toothed margins. The fertile segment is longer than the sterile segment, is branched, and bears grape-like sporangia. Spores germinate underground and develop into minute subterranean, non-photosynthetic gametophytes which depend on an endophytic fungus for nourishment (Vanderhorst 1997).
ecologyComments: May occur in pure stands but generall associated with other Botrychiums
globalRangeComments: Botrychium montanum occurs only in western North America, in Canada and the United States. It occurs in southern Alaska, British Columbia, Washington, northern Idaho, northwestern Montana, Oregon, and northern California. The range extent is estimated to be 1,360,000 square kilometers (Farrar 2011, NatureServe 2021, SEINet 2021). Most of the known occurrences have been reported from Oregon, Montana, California and Washington (NatureServe 2021, SEINet 2021, Vanderhorst 1997).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

county: Bake, Croo, Gran, Harn, Lake, Umat, Unio, Wall, Whee
habitatDescription: Oregon populations are on Quaternary surficial deposits or Hurwal Formation sedimentary bedrock, all sites circumneutral or limy. Favors mesic to marshy openings, and tolerates light shade. In mesic meadows it is in the wettest or shadiest locations. In California and on Mt. Ashland is found with B. simplex in marshy mountain meadows. Tree species predominantly Picea engelmanii in Hurricane basin, and Pinus contorta along lostine River.
physicalDescription: Wavy Moonwort is a small, perennial fern with a single aboveground frond. The frond is usually 10 cm or less tall, yellow-green, and divided into two segments which share a common stalk. The mostly sterile segment is once pinnatifid with usually three or four well separated pairs of thin textured, broadly fan-shaped pinnae which have distinct veins and crenulate margins. The fertile segment is longer than the sterile segment, is branched (often like a tiny Christmas tree), and bears grape-like sporangia. Spores germinate underground and develop into minute, subterranean, non-photosynthetic gametophytes which depend on an endophytic fungus for nourishment.
globalRangeComments: Botrychium crenulatum occurs in western North America from British Columbia, Alberta and northwestern Montana to Arizona and southern California (Farrar 2011). Also reported from Ontario and Newfoundland Island (NatureServe Network Database as of November 2017).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

physicalDescription: Western Moonwort is a small perennial fern with a single erect frond, 3-13 cm high. It is divided into a sterile segment and a fertile segment. The sterile segment has a stalk 0-4 mm long, and a broadly lance-shaped to triangular blade that is pinnately divided with 1-6 pairs of closely adjacent leaflets (pinnae). The basal pinnae are usually partly to wholly pinnately divided and are larger than the lobed or entire-margined upper pinnae. The fertile segment is 2-3 times as long as the sterile segment and 1-3 times pinnately divided into linear segments that bear the spores.
globalRangeComments: Botrychium hesperium ranges from Yukon south through the Rocky Mountains to northern Arizona (Farrar 2011; Gilman et al. 2015). It may also occur in Alaska (Farrar 2011), Saskatchewan (VASCAN 2018), and New Mexico (BONAP 2014). Reports from Michigan, Ontario, and Minnesota, are now identified as Botrychium michiganense (Gilman et al. 2015). Botrychium hesperium may be confused with similar species, especially B. michiganense (in the north) and B. echo (in the south) (Farrar 2011).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

county: Bake, Croo, Doug, Gran, Harn, Hood, Linn, Morr, Umat, Unio, Wall, Wasc, Whee
habitatDescription: Moist meadows, streamsides in coniferous forested areas.
physicalDescription: Mingan Island Moonwort is a small perennial fern with a single aboveground frond. The frond varies in height, but may reach about 20 cm. It is divided into two segments which share a common stalk, and it is usually a deep, dull green and somewhat fleshy. The sterile segment is once pinnatifid with up to 10 usually well separated pairs of pinnae. The pinnae are variable; they are generally narrowly fan-shaped with rounded, entire margined apices, but can be broader and may be lobed or have incised margins. The fertile segment is longer than the sterile segment, is branched, and bears grape-like sporangia. Spores germinate underground and develop into minute subterranean, non-photosynthetic gametophytes which depend on an endophytic fungus for nourishment.
globalRangeComments: One of the most widespread moonworts in North America, occurring in practially all parts of Canada and Alaska and throughout the western United States, south to Arizona, and in all the US/Canadian border states.
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: In mesic meadows along streams or on alluvial fans, on or near sedimentary bedrock in the Hurwal or Martin Bridge Formation. Possibly ground water is circumneutral or limy. Typically many strawberries near, surrounding forests Picea engelmannii. Colonies in full sun or where they receive some shade from nearby trees. In wettest site, a marshy meadow, Botrychiums are on dry hummocks.
physicalDescription: Upward-lobed Moonwort is a small, perennial fern with a single aboveground frond. The frond is usually about 10 cm tall, yellow-green, and divided into two segments which share a common stalk. The mostly sterile segment is once pinnatifid with up to six pairs of strongly ascending, narrowly triangular pinnae which have deeply lacerate margins. The sterile segment often has a few sporangia on the margins of the pinnae or on small branches. The fertile segment is longer than the sterile segment, is branched, and bears grape-like sporangia. Spores germinate underground and develop into minute, subterranean, non-photosynthetic gametophytes which depend on an endophytic fungus for nourishment.
ecologyComments: Species hopscotches between openings in the forest, which may have been maintained historically by fire.
globalRangeComments: Botrychium ascendens occurs in western, northern and northeastern North America, in the United States and Canada. It occurs from southern Alaska and southwestern Yukon Territory, south at higher elevations in the mountains of California, southern Nevada, Montana, Wyoming and Colorado, across Canada to Newfoundland, and in northern Minnesota, and New England in the United States. The range extent is estimated to be 12.5 million square kilometers (CNDDB 2022, GBIF 2022, iNaturalist 2022, NatureServe 2022, SEINet 2022).
references: Kartesz, J.T. 1994. A synonymized checklist of the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland. 2nd edition. 2 vols. Timber Press, Portland, OR.

habitatDescription: Each population is on Quaternary surficial deposits, two close to sedimentary rocks of Hurwal Formation, which may be limy. All may be influenced by circumneutral or calcareaous ground water. Sites are open stands of Pinus contorta among low herbaceous growth, mostly Fragaria virginiana. Sites are sunny most of the day, with some early and late shade. Soil on average is mesic.
physicalDescription: Stalked moonwort is a perennial with a single above ground frond up to 25 cm tall. It is divided into two segments that share a common stalk. The lower common stalk is usually reddish brown and the upper part of the plant is a dull green. The mostly sterile segment is conspicuously stalked and once to twice pinnatifid with up to five pairs of primary pinnae. The pinnae have irregular lobes and vary from pinnatifid to bifid to narrowly fan shaped and the lower ones often bear sporangia. The fertile segment is longer than the sterile segment and bears grape-like sporangia that contain thousands of spores; larger plants usually have two large ascending lateral branches.
globalRangeComments: Occurs in northcentral and northeastern Washington, northeastern Oregon, central California, northern Idaho, northwestern Montana, west-central (Skeena River) and east-central (Quesnel area) British Columbia, two widely separated locations in southern Alberta (southwestern AB adjacent to MT occurrences and southeastern AB near SK border), and southern Saskatchewan. Disjunct occurrences are known from the Alaska peninsula and northern Quebec.
